item.title: Okta Links ShinyHunters-Associated Vishing Group to New INCEPTION Data Leak Site
item.description:
Okta tracks O-UNC-053, a vishing cluster tied to ShinyHunters, which now appears to operate under a new data leak site called INCEPTION. Operators call targets, harvest credentials and MFA codes through tailored phishing pages, take over SaaS accounts, and extort for stolen data. Okta has tracked the cluster since March 2026.
- Rebrand signal: Okta says victims of O-UNC-053 were previously posted on the ShinyHunters leak site. As of November 16, 2026, INCEPTION began listing data from the same targets. The ShinyHunters site went offline in late September 2026 after the arrest of three alleged members, including a Canadian 🇨🇦 co-conspirator tied to the FBI jobs portal breach. Okta saw no leak-site postings for this cluster from early September through early November, a gap it calls consistent with prior shifts by Com-affiliated actors. INCEPTION publicly denies any ShinyHunters link, and Okta says the true relationship and the authenticity of the posted data are unconfirmed.
- Attack chain: operators phone the victim while the victim sits on a phishing page. They coach the victim into entering credentials, reading out one-time passcodes, and approving push notifications. Once in, they access SaaS applications, exfiltrate data, and threaten to publish it. The kit intercepts authentication flows but is not built to defeat phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys and Okta FastPass. Targets span technology, healthcare, biotech, financial services, insurance, entertainment, gaming, retail, transportation, hospitality, and legal.
- Infrastructure patterns: domains are registered through NiceNIC, Spaceship, Tucows, and NameSilo. Okta lists four naming patterns: legal-<target>[.]com, legaldept-<target>[.]com, <target>[.]legal, and a target name followed by -legal on the .com TLD. The legal theme began in October 2026, and these domains are often registered on or within a day of a campaign starting. Earlier waves used help desk, support, and claims themes. Okta observed victim names appear on the ShinyHunters leak site 1 to 28 days after the phishing domain was registered.
- Confirmed domains linked to the activity: legal-pepsico[.]com, legal-paychex[.]com, legal-duolingo[.]com, activisionblizzard-legal[.]com, legal-westernunion[.]com, legal-dropbox[.]com, legal-indeed[.]com, legal-creditkarma[.]com, legal-amd[.]com, legal-grubhub[.]com, and legal-twitch[.]tv. Unit 42 has seen more than 70 legal-themed .com domains since October 2026 across crypto, finance, healthcare, high tech, and hospitality.
- Filtering behavior: ReversingLabs' Robert Simmons says the domains are registered in rapid evening batches and sit behind Cloudflare. A filtered kit shows tailored content only to intended victims and routes other visitors to the target organization's real Okta or NetIQ sign-in flow. That means a casual check of the URL may show a legitimate login page, so scanners and analysts can miss the lure.
Takeaway: if you are tied to any sector above, check your own brand and your vendors' names against the legal-<target> and <target>-legal patterns in newly registered domain feeds and certificate data. Since the kit relays OTPs and push approvals, your best evidence is in identity provider records: look for MFA approvals or OTP sign-ins that coincide with a help desk or legal-themed call to the user, followed by unusual SaaS access and bulk data export. Interview the user for call timing and the URL they visited, and preserve the phone and browser history before they are overwritten. Use the confirmed domains above as starting points, and moving privileged users to passkeys or FastPass closes the gap this kit cannot cross.

item.title: Iran-Aligned Volant Manticore Uses IPFS-Based KuboShell Backdoor in Espionage Campaigns
item.description:
Iran-aligned Volant Manticore, likely ex-MuddyWater operators, is targeting Cyprus telecoms, airlines and critical infrastructure with KuboShell, a backdoor that uses IPFS for C2, and the Homa framework.
- Check Point says the cluster has been active since late August 2025. Lures include bogus CVs built on AI-generated personas, with a link to "download the full resume" that deploys KuboShell. One target was a Cyprus-based airline flying Cyprus to Israel 🇮🇱. Credential-harvesting campaigns also collect email and corporate logins from impersonated organizations.
- KuboShell is a Windows backdoor using Pinata to move files over IPFS. It checks for admin rights and tries to relaunch itself elevated, triggering a UAC prompt, if it lacks them. It takes the MAC address of the first network adapter as the victim ID, then registers by uploading a file containing "hi", saved as C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token.
- Tasking is file-based. KuboShell polls Pinata every 60 seconds for <MAC>.txt, resolves the IPFS identifier, pulls the content through Pinata's public gateway and runs it in a hidden PowerShell window. The backdoor does not capture output. Results come back only if the command writes them to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt, which is then uploaded. It is used mainly for recon before a stronger payload lands.
- That payload is Homa, a JavaScript reimplementation of the MuddyC2Go client, which lets the operators keep the older server-side component. Stage 1 is a PowerShell stager contacting 185.205.187[.]109:8000 to fetch a loader in memory. Stage 2 decodes and launches a JavaScript backdoor. Stage 3 loops C2 and runs PowerShell, SSH and cmd.exe commands. The report does not identify the follow-on modules. Homa was also delivered via a macro-enabled Word file, MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc, aimed at a Cypriot defense-related government entity. Its VBA backdoor runs follow-up payloads through cmd.exe.
- RMM tooling travels alongside: MeshCentral, NetLock RMM and N-able RMM. In September 2026 a phishing wave hit Saudi 🇸🇦 healthcare targets with AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip (backdoor) and Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip (N-able RMM). Some emails came from a compromised account at a private Saudi 🇸🇦 hospital. Check Point ties the Saudi 🇸🇦 pivot to rising Saudi-Houthi hostilities and notes MOIS has a record of targeting healthcare during conflicts.
- Attribution: both Volant Manticore and MuddyWater are assessed as MOIS-affiliated. Check Point believes Volant Manticore is former MuddyWater operators who split off, possibly around 2023 when MuddyWater moved from MuddyC2Go to DarkBeatC2.
Takeaway: hunt Public folders for <MAC>.log and <MAC>re.txt pairs, hidden-window PowerShell spawned by an unfamiliar process, and roughly 60-second polling to Pinata for <MAC>.txt, with downloads via its public IPFS gateway when tasked. Also search proxy and firewall logs for 185.205.187[.]109:8000, and inventory unexpected MeshCentral, NetLock or N-able agents. For the macro lure, review Office child processes running cmd.exe. Preserve any hard-coded Pinata token you recover from a sample, since it ties victims to the operator's storage.

item.title: The first hour after an impossible-travel alert
item.description:
An impossible-travel alert is a question, not a verdict. VPNs, mobile carriers and cloud proxies produce the same pattern, so the first hour is about proving or disproving compromise from the sign-in record, then containing in a set order if it is confirmed.
- Start with the sign-in record itself. In Microsoft Entra ID, pull it with Get-MgAuditLogSignIn or from the sign-in logs. Note ResultType, which tells you whether the sign-in actually succeeded, plus the client app, the user agent, and the device ID if the device is registered. A failed second sign-in and a successful one are very different cases.
- Read the conditional access result carefully. Report-only policies log a result but do not block, so a "would have blocked" entry does not mean the attacker was stopped. A policy in the "not applied" state means no conditions matched. Record which policy applied (or didn't) before you decide what the attacker could reach.
- Scope the second address before you act. The report's example has the second sign-in from 203.0.113[.]45, resolving to login-verify[.]example at the time of the event. Run the same filter across SigninLogs for the last 24 hours (TimeGenerated, IPAddress, project UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResultType) to see whether the address touched other accounts. The report notes its IP is a documentation-range placeholder, so swap in the live indicator.
- Once the account is confirmed compromised, the report gives a fixed order. First revoke active sessions and refresh tokens. Then reset the password and require MFA re-registration. Then block the IP at the edge and in conditional access. Revoking tokens before the reset matters because a password change alone does not end a session the attacker already holds.
- Review mailbox rules created in the window. Start with forwarding to external addresses, then rules that move or delete messages on arrival. These are the quiet persistence and concealment mechanisms that outlast a password reset.
- Before closing, check the device the user normally signs in from. Look for new entries under %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ and for scheduled tasks created in the same window as the suspicious sign-in.
Practitioner takeaway: write the first hour down before you need it. Capture who made each call and when in the case record, since each tool is right about its own slice and blind to the rest. Pivot on the source IP across 24 hours of sign-ins, treat mailbox rules and endpoint persistence as part of the same case, and don't close until the user's usual device has been checked. The KQL example and the indicators are in the report.

item.title: Remus Stealer Uses a Fake Google Sheets Extension to Steal Gmail Messages
item.description:
Remus Stealer drops a Chrome extension posing as Google Sheets (v0.5.4). It reads Gmail through the victim's logged-in session and posts sender, subject, and body to hxxps://prem1um[.]onl/m. This may explain how mailbox access outlives the stealer executable.
Invoke RE found the extension and Gen Threat Labs analyzed the delivery module. Hudson Rock has not reproduced any of it.
- Install chain: Invoke RE reports Remus drops a ZIP in the Windows temp directory, unpacks it with PowerShell Expand-Archive, then backs up and modifies Chrome's Secure Preferences to register an unpacked extension and enable developer mode. Gen Threat Labs found a DLL carrying the ZIP in its data section. The module arrives through Remus's dynamic configuration, so it can vary between builds. It edits Preferences or Secure Preferences and recalculates the integrity values.
- The extension: it calls itself Google Sheets, with an offline document editing description and no spreadsheet interface. It has a background service worker, storage and alarms permissions, and <all_urls> host access. Reported extension IDs are cfmepkojgnkahbmgablgdahdomjdppgf (Invoke RE and Gen) and mgggekjcdcdaiagafcbdhcdapifehhmc (Gen).
- Collection: a reported one-minute loop checks Gmail account slots 0 through 9 via the unread Atom feed, then fetches individual messages. Gen describes MIME retrieval without attachment exfiltration. The browser attaches the existing session to the request, so no cookie database export is needed. This happens after login, so it is not an MFA bypass. But captured recovery links or emailed verification codes could help attackers reach other services. Checking ten slots does not prove ten compromised accounts.
- What persistence means here: a password change or session revocation should stop interception, but the extension stays installed. Per Gen, a later sign-in in that browser can restore access. Not established: a Gmail zero-day, collection while all Chrome processes are stopped, or fresh-mail theft after verified removal and full account recovery. prem1um[.]onl also appears in the native Remus C2 configuration, which links the implant to the collection endpoint.
- Hunt artifacts: look for %TEMP%\cfmepkojgnkahbmgablgdahdomjdppgf[.]zip and the unpacked directory %TEMP%\cfmepkojgnkahbmgablgdahdomjdppgf\. Also check a suspicious process spawning PowerShell to unpack an archive, then unexpected writes to Secure Preferences, Preferences, and .bak backups. A Google Sheets extension loading from a temp path with developer mode on is a strong lead. DNS or hostname telemetry can surface the domain. Seeing the /m path needs endpoint or decrypted HTTP telemetry. Developer mode, PowerShell, and unpacked extensions all have legitimate uses, so correlate several signals.
Takeaway: before remediation, preserve the ZIP, the extracted extension (manifest.json and worker files), the Chrome profile config, and process and network records. Inspect every Chrome profile on the host, not just the default one. Then revoke sessions and change passwords from a trusted device, remove the extension, clean or rebuild the host, and only then resume sign-ins. Review mailbox forwarding, filters, and delegation, and reassess services whose reset links or codes landed in the mailbox. Gen's SHA-256 hashes for the DLL, ZIP, and extension JavaScript are in the report. Hudson Rock has not verified them, and they should not be mapped one-to-one to the IDs or Invoke RE's endpoint. Treat exact ID matches as leads, but also hunt behavior and artifacts that can change between builds.

Then revoke sessions and change passwords from a trusted device, remove the extension, clean or rebuild the host, and only then resume sign-ins. Review mailbox forwarding, filters, and delegation, and reassess services whose reset links or codes landed in the mailbox. Gen's SHA-256 hashes for the DLL, ZIP, and extension JavaScript are in the report. Hudson Rock has not verified them, and they should not be mapped one-to-one to the IDs or Invoke RE's endpoint. Treat exact ID matches as leads, but also hunt behavior and artifacts that can change between builds.

item.title: Cisco Expressway RCE (CVE-2026-76466) Exploited for Root Access
item.description:
Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 9.8) gives unauthenticated root RCE on clustered nodes. It is exploited in the wild, listed in CISA KEV, and one intrusion pivoted from edge nodes into a Russian 🇷🇺 network.
- The flaw: CVE-2026-76466 is mapped to CWE-798 (hard-coded credentials), CVSS v3.1 9.8. The cluster database service relies on persistent cookies, and client certificates are not validated properly when TLS Verify Mode is enabled for clustering. An attacker with network access who holds those cookies can connect to the database service, invoke specific RPC commands and run commands as root. No credentials or user interaction are needed. Cisco does not publish the cookie values or the RPC sequence.
- Scope: Expressway-C and Expressway-E, virtual and appliance, only when clustered. X15.5.3 and earlier are vulnerable, X15.5.20 fixes it, and X14 and earlier have no fix in that train, so those devices need migration. Cisco offers no workaround. Public exploit code with a detection script is on GitHub. Its author tested only a two-node Expressway-C X15.3.2 cluster. The repo describes the vulnerable TLS mode differently from Cisco, so do not clear a clustered node on its TLS setting alone.
- Exploitation status: CISA added it to KEV on November 20, 2026, with a federal remediation deadline of November 23. Cisco's advisory still says PSIRT was not aware of malicious use, which now lags the evidence. F6 documented what it calls possibly the first in-the-wild case: an unnamed Russian 🇷🇺 organization running X15.5.3. Attackers exploited two internet-facing Expressway devices, ran commands as root, then reached two more cluster nodes on the internal network. No actor attribution. KEV confirms exploitation, not scale, and no exposed-device count has been published.
- Post-exploitation: custom Python scripts scanned the network, enumerated SMB resources, talked to SQL Server and WinRM, and reached GitLab repositories to collect credentials and sensitive data. F6 assesses from code comments and fix notes that the scripts were possibly written with AI help.
- Researcher-observed indicators, not Cisco-published: IPs 66.179.31[.]32 and 18.130.47[.]116, the log artifact wombat@127.0.0[.]1 in erlang.log, and Python scripts under /mnt/harddisk/i{0-9}{4}[a-zA-Z]?/*.py.
Takeaway: inventory which Expressway-C and Expressway-E nodes are clustered, then hunt the edge nodes first. Check erlang.log for the wombat artifact and the file system for scripts matching that path pattern. Look for connections to the cluster database service from addresses that are not cluster peers. Expressway nodes rarely need outbound SMB, SQL Server, WinRM or GitLab traffic, so any of it is a strong signal. Root access lets an attacker alter local logs, so a clean result is not proof the device was never touched. Lean on network and internal telemetry. Check GitLab and internal logins for credentials that were reachable from these nodes.
If compromise is suspected, treat the whole cluster as untrusted, rebuild from known-good images, and rotate reachable credentials, tokens and repository secrets. Upgrade to X15.5.20. If you must wait, F6's stopgap is to allow TCP 4371 and 4372 only from trusted cluster node IPs. That is not a Cisco workaround and does not replace the patch.

item.title: Machine-Generated Fake Plugin Turns WordPress Sites Into JavaScript Delivery Points
item.description:
A name-generator-built fake WordPress plugin turns infected sites into a same-origin JavaScript delivery platform for anonymous visitors. It proxies attacker C2 through the victim's own domain, stays dormant for logged-in users, and includes an auth backdoor and timestomping.
Wordfence recovered it in two incident response cleanups, January 2026 and September 2026. Names are machine-made prefix + tech word + suffix compounds (trijavascriptly, ultravueal, maxdataic), plus 8-character files like 5auul2bn.php and yv6b6sff.js. Roughly two-thirds of each file is filler comments and unreachable functions.
- Delivery chain: a visitor loads any page, then a POST to /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php?action=<generated> returns a CID and a 5-minute cookie, then a POST to /wp-json/<plugin>-<6 random chars>/v1/<route> returns JavaScript. The plugin calls the C2 server-side and injects the response as a script tag in the document head. The browser only talks to the victim's own domain and TLS cert, so CSP, extensions, and client-side blocklists see same-origin traffic.
- C2: one config constant starting with 2$ is base64-decoded twice to reveal kiloporotolimo[.]com. linearprocesshost[.]com appeared in an earlier version and juioprtexi[.]com in a separate infection. The January build hardcoded the C2 and used an AJAX nonce gate. The September build encodes it and uses a cookie-gated REST route. The payload looks like ad fraud or traffic resale (a /api/click conversion call), with no PHP-side DB queries, file reads, or outbound data theft observed.
- Inverted access control: every entry point checks is_user_logged_in() and bails for admins and other logged-in users. That lowers detection risk for the operator and means the owner may never see the behavior while logged in.
- Persistence and evasion: a 64KB helper file holds only 72 lines of code hidden in filler comments. A function on the init hook takes two GET parameters, a user ID and a hardcoded password, then calls wp_set_auth_cookie for that user and redirects to /wp-admin. Password resets and 2FA do not stop it while the plugin exists. The plugin also removes itself from the plugins screen via the all_plugins filter.
- Timestomping and intrusion vector: the plugin copies the oldest mtime among installed plugins onto its own directory and files, so every file carries the same modification time down to the second. That is unusual, since real zip extraction spreads times over seconds to minutes. The timestomp is registered via register_activation_hook and gated on current_user_can('administrator'), so seeing it points to a compromised admin account activating the plugin. Installs via file write plus active_plugins edits or wp-cli would not timestomp.
Hunting and triage:
- Pull the REST index and look for a namespace shaped like <generated-plugin-name>-<6 random chars>/v1. WordPress publishes every registered namespace, so anyone can check.
- Search access logs for the triple from one IP in quick succession: GET any page, POST admin-ajax.php, POST the wp-json plugin route.
- Compare mtimes across wp-content/plugins and flag directories where every file shares an identical timestamp. Check error logs for paths like wp-content/plugins/platformist-quadendpointer-1/class/pentatypescriptly-multireacter.php, where WordPress appended -1 because the directory already existed.
- Observed plugin directory names are listed in the report: framework-triappment, platformist-quadendpointer, ultraapiist-pentajavascripter, uniserviceist-multiinfrastructure, laravel-janet, smartrestal-serverful, miniapplicationing-protypescriptic, idatasion-fasttypescriptor.
Takeaway: if you find one, treat the admin account as the intrusion point. Preserve admin login history, then review for other admin users and sessions. Resetting passwords is not enough while the plugin, including its init-hook backdoor file, remains, and the plugin will not appear in the plugins screen, so inspect the filesystem directly. Plugin directory names and C2 domains are in the report.

item.title: Exposing the Gmail “Zero-Day” Behind Remus Stealer’s Email Interception Feature
item.description:
Remus Stealer's "Gmail zero-day" is not a zero-day. Gen Threat Labs found a module that silently installs a malicious Chrome extension, which reads mail through the victim's live Gmail session. Revoke the sessions and the interception stops, but the extension stays installed.
- The claim and the reality: on November 8, 2026, the Remus developers advertised mailbox access that survives password changes and session revocation. Gen Threat Labs found no Gmail flaw. The extension's requests all ride on the victim's existing session, so signing out or revoking sessions halts it. The risk is that victims do not notice the extension, and it resumes as soon as they sign back in.
- Delivery: the interceptor is not in the core stealer. Remus pulls its dynamic config from C2 in several parts, each encrypted with ChaCha20 (32-byte key and 8-byte nonce prepended). Values inside are Base64 plus a 4-byte XOR key. The stealer maps the decoded module into its own address space on a new thread. It appears only in some builds, probably tied to subscription tier. The module is a native x64 DLL that targets Chrome only, with the extension ZIP stored unencrypted in .rdata.
- Install chain: Chrome 137 dropped --load-extension, so Remus edits the profile instead. Order of events: 1. Drop %TEMP%\<extension_id>.zip. 2. Run powershell Expand-Archive into %TEMP%\<extension_id>. 3. Parse Local State and enumerate profile[.]info_cache. 4. Pick Secure Preferences or Preferences by comparing %USERDOMAIN% to GetComputerNameA(). 5. Register the extension under extensions.settings.<extension_id>. 6. Set extensions.ui.developer_mode to true. 7. Recompute protection.macs with HMAC-SHA-256 (plus protection.super_mac for Secure Preferences). 8. Write a .bak backup of the original file. 9. Kill chrome.exe, write the file, and, if Chrome was running, relaunch it with --restore-last-session. The MAC technique is old, documented by Kaimi in 2015 and revisited by Synacktiv in 2025.
- The extension: disguised as Google Sheets, with a description copied from Google Docs Offline. It requests <all_urls>, storage and alarms, and runs in an obfuscator.io-style obfuscated service worker. Every minute it queries the Gmail Atom feed at /mail/u/<index>/feed/atom for indexes 0 to 9 with credentials included, then fetches each unread message as raw MIME via the ?view=att&th=<id>&attid=0 endpoint. It POSTs subject, decoded text, sender, victim address and a hardcoded campaign build ID to C2 over HTTPS. Attachment names and contents are not sent. Failed sends retry with exponential backoff, and sent IDs are tracked in chrome[.]storage.local.
- Visible traces: the victim sees only an unpacked-icon extension card and Developer Mode switched on. Malicious extension IDs from the report: cfmepkojgnkahbmgablgdahdomjdppgf and mgggekjcdcdaiagafcbdhcdapifehhmc.
Takeaway: after any infostealer hit, resetting passwords and revoking sessions is not enough. Audit every Chrome profile for unpacked extensions and Developer Mode enabled. Check the extensions.settings entries in Preferences and Secure Preferences for the IDs above or a fake "Google Sheets" with <all_urls>. Look for Preferences.bak or Secure Preferences.bak beside the originals, %TEMP%\<extension_id>.zip leftovers, and a PowerShell Expand-Archive into %TEMP% shortly before chrome.exe was killed and relaunched with --restore-last-session. Remove the extension before the user signs back in to Gmail. Hashes for the DLL modules, extension ZIPs and extension.js are in the report's IoC section.

item.title: ScreenConnect Flaw CVE-2026-84869 Exploited
item.description:
Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9) in the ConnectWise ScreenConnect host client. A guest joins a support session and runs files on the MSP technician's workstation with no prompt. Patching the server does not close it.
- The flaw: improper privilege management and missing authorization in the host client. In Support and Access sessions, a guest with file-transfer rights can trigger transfers and run the file with elevated rights, and the technician only has to join. ConnectWise fixed it in 26.6.5 (bulletin dated September 8, 2026). CISA added it to KEV on September 11, 2026, with a September 14 deadline that formally binds U.S. 🇺🇸 federal civilian agencies only. ConnectWise says servers are not impacted; the issue affects both cloud and on-prem deployments because the vulnerable code runs on each technician's machine. Host clients on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 builds were still in use weeks after the fix.
- Confirmed compromise (Huntress, November 12): a guest pushed update_224ac089.bat and the technician's client ran it from its Temp folder. Within about nine seconds the script relaunched hidden via PowerShell, reported the victim to a Telegram bot, ran recon, pulled a second-stage MSI from masterdarky[.]com, unpacked it under %LOCALAPPDATA%, enabled the Secondary Logon service, and launched a rebranded ScreenConnect client, WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe. That client connected to the attacker's relay on port 8041. The result is attacker-owned remote access on a machine MSP staff use to reach customer environments. A harmless marker.txt ran on a second technician's client on November 13, which the researchers read as a test.
- Scale: from October 20 to November 16, guests sent about 688,000 run-file requests for update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat to 42 MSP servers from 29 source IPs. Sessions used blank names or default-looking hostnames, and many set the Company field to "crypto client." Researchers assess with high confidence that the spray operator also controls masterdarky[.]com. No named actor is linked. More targeted attempts on October 23, 24 and 27 pushed Sync.bat into three real customer sessions, using path traversal to land it in the technician's Startup folder. These counts are exposure and attempts, not confirmed compromises.
- Don't conflate it with two nearby campaigns. SCKit (first seen November 11) installed rogue clients on at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations via legitimate cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances, and its RelayTrap component tries to send a payload back to technicians who connect to an infected endpoint. Crypto-named decoy sessions hit at least 118 self-hosted servers at 109 organizations, with no file transfer or execution observed. Researchers disagree on whether SCKit shares this trust boundary, and Huntress treats it as separate. ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions across about 400 partner environments and warned that this does not remove access already established.
- Hunt on the server first: in a copy of App_Data\Session.db, look for RanFiles or SentFiles events from guest connections. Key on repeated update*.bat, marker.txt, Run-Lateral.bat, svc_payload.cmd, or any path containing ../, then check whether a technician was connected at that moment. On workstations, look for the ScreenConnect client spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe or wscript.exe for scripts in its Temp folder, unknown Startup items (especially Sync.bat), folders named %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<8 hex>, and %TEMP%\wupdate_<8 hex>.msi. On the network, look for ScreenConnect relay connections, often on port 8041, to domains the MSP does not own.
IOCs from the report: masterdarky[.]com (payload host and rogue relay) 194.15.36[.]33 (relay domain resolution) SHA-256 of WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe: f8871b1561d5c77c297378a7f49c84de52a01ff297395544f0e95d13ef972841 91.224.92[.]83 and 91.224.92[.]167 (guests pushing Run-Lateral.bat and marker.txt) 193.26.115[.]63 and 57.128.131[.]66 (guests pushing Sync.bat via path traversal) 107.148.223[.]37 (guest pushing svc_payload.cmd)
Takeaway: a clean Session.db search does not prove a technician was never exposed, since it only shows what was requested and logged. Detection guidance and the full spray source IP list are in the Huntress report. Update every host client and listed Access agent to 26.6.5 or later, and use the server's connection history to find stragglers. If clients can't be updated yet, remove the TransferFiles permission. If a workstation was hit, isolate it, remove the rogue client and its files, restore the Secondary Logon service's normal start type, and rotate every credential reachable from it: RMM, PSA, ScreenConnect, password vault, and customer admin accounts.

On workstations, look for the ScreenConnect client spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe or wscript.exe for scripts in its Temp folder, unknown Startup items (especially Sync.bat), folders named %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<8 hex>, and %TEMP%\wupdate_<8 hex>.msi. On the network, look for ScreenConnect relay connections, often on port 8041, to domains the MSP does not own.

IOCs from the report:
masterdarky[.]com (payload host and rogue relay)
194.15.36[.]33 (relay domain resolution)
SHA-256 of WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe: f8871b1561d5c77c297378a7f49c84de52a01ff297395544f0e95d13ef972841
91.224.92[.]83 and 91.224.92[.]167 (guests pushing Run-Lateral.bat and marker.txt)
193.26.115[.]63 and 57.128.131[.]66 (guests pushing Sync.bat via path traversal)
107.148.223[.]37 (guest pushing svc_payload.cmd)

Takeaway: a clean Session.db search does not prove a technician was never exposed, since it only shows what was requested and logged. Detection guidance and the full spray source IP list are in the Huntress report. Update every host client and listed Access agent to 26.6.5 or later, and use the server's connection history to find stragglers. If clients can't be updated yet, remove the TransferFiles permission. If a workstation was hit, isolate it, remove the rogue client and its files, restore the Secondary Logon service's normal start type, and rotate every credential reachable from it: RMM, PSA, ScreenConnect, password vault, and customer admin accounts.

item.title: Volant Manticore: Flying Under the Radar
item.description:
Iranian 🇮🇷 group Volant Manticore, likely ex-MuddyWater operators, targets Cyprus airlines and telecoms with KuboShell, an IPFS-C2 backdoor, then pivots hard to Saudi Arabia 🇸🇦 healthcare.
- Check Point Research ties the cluster to MOIS with medium confidence. Activity traces back to September 2025. The first sample was a fake CV from "Athena Marinou," an AI-generated Cyprus travel professional, aimed at an airline flying Cyprus-Israel routes. The link behind the CV text pulls an archive from hxxps://files.catbox[.]moe/hnrhw9.zip that delivers KuboShell. In September 2026 the Saudi 🇸🇦 wave used AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip, plus a sibling archive carrying an N-able RMM executable. The email account tied to the sample belongs to a private Saudi 🇸🇦 hospital, likely compromised with leaked credentials.
- KuboShell is a 64-bit backdoor that uses IPFS through the Pinata pinning service for C2. It uses the first adapter's MAC as the victim ID and registers by uploading a "hi" file saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log. Every 60 seconds it checks Pinata for <MAC>.txt, runs the contents in hidden PowerShell, and uploads C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt if the command wrote results there. Operator history shows quser, whoami, ipconfig, then a download of Install-Remotely.ps1 (a NetLock RMM installer) from remote.medochomie[.]com. It acts as a guardrail before the real payload.
- That payload is the Homa Framework. Stage 1 is a PowerShell stager that fetches hxxp://185.205.187[.]109:8000/{UID} and runs it with Invoke-Expression. Stage 2 XOR-decodes a JScript blob and compiles it with Add-Type. Stage 3 is a JavaScript backdoor using WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1, POSTing "hi" to /X{key} in a {content}(){key} format. Commands prefixed "function" run in hidden PowerShell; others run through cmd.exe /c with output staged in C:\Users\Public\outputt2.txt, and the loop sleeps 10 seconds. It is a reimplementation of the MuddyC2Go client, so the old server side keeps working. Operator commands list, persist, and payload match MuddyWater C2 frameworks like PhonyC2.
- The January 2026 lure MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc, likely aimed at a Cypriot government entity, shows the VBA path. The macro sets HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Word\Security\AccessVBOM to 1 and rebuilds stage two in a hidden Word instance. It then kills every other WINWORD.EXE so Word appears to crash. It registers with 185.205.187[.]108:25498 over plain HTTP, drops files into C:\Users\Public, and stages command output in C:\ProgramData\UiAutomation.txt. Commands starting with $uri or req run through PowerShell, matching Homa stager variables.
- Infrastructure splits into RMM management (MeshCentral, then NetLock RMM) and credential harvesting with GoPhish. federation.aegeneair[.]com mirrors the Aegean Airlines ADFS sign-in subdomain. For Saudi 🇸🇦 targets the group reused cnpcyprus[.]net as NetLock C2, then re-pointed it on October 11 to a Saudi 🇸🇦 HostZealot VPS at 185.253.118[.]221. That server exposed an open Python SimpleHTTPServer directory on port 4444, which matches a MuddyWater server. Other attribution evidence: operator activity fits UTC+3:30 with a Thursday-Friday weekend, and the KuboShell PDB path includes F:\homa\.
Takeaway: hunt for hidden PowerShell that pulls from a bare IP and pipes to Invoke-Expression. Hunt for files named <MAC>.log and <MAC>re.txt in C:\Users\Public, and for non-browser processes talking to Pinata's gateway. On Word hosts, look for AccessVBOM set to 1 followed by mass WINWORD.EXE termination. Audit for unsanctioned NetLock, N-able, or MeshCentral agents. Hashes, IPs, domains, and email IOCs are in the report.

item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: VMware vCenter SRP Authentication Bypass to Root (CVE-2026-123890)
item.description:
CVE-2026-123890: unauthenticated SRP session-key theft on VMware vCenter's DCE/RPC interface chains to root shell with no password, no hash, and no admin required to be online.
Rapid7's report walks through a full exploit chain against vCenter Server Appliance 8.0.2.00400 (build 23929136, Photon OS 4.0) that starts with a single unauthenticated TCP connection to port 2012 and ends at uid=0(root). The root cause is two independent failures that combine badly: a session-key getter that returns the SRP shared secret before the client proves it knows the password, and an RPC context resolver that looks up handles in a process-wide table with no check that the requesting connection owns that context.
- Two bugs, one chain. The SRP getter in vmdir (Srv_rpc_srp_verifier_get_session_key in rpcsrpserv.c) checks only that the verifier and key are non-null, never that the caller authenticated or owns the verifier. The underlying SRP library (srp_verifier_get_session_key in csrp/srp.c) does not consult the authenticated flag before returning the key. Separately, the RPC context resolver (rpc_ss_ee_ctx_from_wire in ctxeectx.c) takes a UUID from the wire, searches a process-wide table, and returns the associated context with no identity comparison against the connection that created it. Rapid7 confirmed this directly: one anonymous connection created a verifier, and a second anonymous connection retrieved that verifier's session key before any password proof was sent.
- Context handles are UUIDv1 values derived from gettimeofday output (uuid__get_os_time in uuidsys.c), so only the timestamp component varies across newly created contexts. The attacker creates a reference verifier immediately before initiating a GSS-API login as administrator[@]vsphere.local and another immediately after, bounding the hidden login handle's timestamp. In Rapid7's standalone test the interval spanned 115,610 UUID ticks (about 11.56 milliseconds). Four workers recovered the pending login's handle in 5,083 queries in roughly 0.88 seconds.
- With the session key in hand, the attacker computes the normal SRP client proof and verifies the server's response with no password input. Packet-protection keys are derived using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 (principal as salt, 128 iterations, 64-byte output) feeding AES-CBC and HMAC-SHA1. That authenticated RPC session reaches the database-copy interface (vmdirdbcp, interface UUID 72c780fe-af6b-42ba-9b02-f61f4ccc98ed), which passes its own access check because the caller is now authenticated as the SSO administrator. The attacker requests /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb (Rapid7's first export was 16.22 MB). The TenantCredential-1 record contains the STS RSA private key. A forged SAML assertion signed with that key authenticates to the vCenter REST API as administrator[@]vsphere.local, which is then used to create a local superAdmin OS account, enable SSH and Bash, and reach a root shell via the sudo rule in /etc/sudoers.d/applmgmt. This final stage also uses TCP 443 and TCP 22 in addition to TCP 2012.
- Rapid7 identifies several log sources that survive this attack. In /var/log/vmware/vmdird/vmdird-syslog.log, look for "Remote DB transfer (/storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) granted." In /var/log/vmware/vapi/endpoint/endpoint-access.log, look for POST /rest/com/vmware/cis/session, POST /rest/appliance/local-accounts/ returning HTTP 200, and PUT requests to /rest/appliance/access/ssh and /rest/appliance/access/shell. In /var/log/vmware/applmgmt/applmgmt.log, look for local account creation attributed to Administrator[@]VSPHERE.LOCAL paired with SSH and Bash enablement. In /var/log/audit/sshinfo.log and its rotated, gzip-compressed copies, look for password authentication for an unexpected account followed immediately by sudo /bin/bash -i. Linux audit.log retains EXECVE records for useradd with -G superAdmin and the sudo -n /bin/bash -i invocation.
Practitioner takeaway: start triage at vmdird-syslog.log for the data.mdb transfer grant, then pivot to applmgmt.log for account creation and SSH/Bash enablement timestamps, then to endpoint-access.log for the source IP and user-agent of the API session, and finally to sshinfo.log (including rotated .gz copies) and audit.log for the SSH login, sudo escalation, and useradd arguments. The database-copy grant, local superAdmin creation, SSH enablement, and an immediate sudo /bin/bash -i in close sequence are the correlation pattern. Legitimate directory replication can also trigger the database-copy grant, so sequence and fit to expected change windows matter. Patch to vCenter 8.0 U3m per VMSA-2026-0009, and restrict port 2012 to only the systems that require it.

item.title: LATAM’s Financial Fraud Ecosystem: Key Threats and Strategies for Business Protection
item.description:
Brazilian-linked financial fraud runs as a modular chain of interchangeable services, not one gang or one malware family. Takedowns of Grandoreiro and Lumma displaced activity rather than ending it, so ANY.RUN's report argues for hunting shared behaviors instead of family names.
- Delivery and execution: Invoice lures with the .php?tipo=inv pattern sit on domains like 2026pdf[.]com, impdocw[.]com and otxsmart[.]com, hosted in a Germany 🇩🇪 IP range, plus share[.]google links with Roundcube parameters that suggest compromised webmail. Compromised legitimate Brazilian 🇧🇷 WordPress-style sites (santacasabarbacena[.]com[.]br, clinicadoutor10[.]com[.]br, bioanalisemaracaju[.]com[.]br) push ClickFix, and newer variants pull configs from smart contracts (EtherHiding). In the "pix" query of 390 analyses, ClickFix showed in 13% and EtherHiding in 12%. Banking Trojans Mispadu/URSA, Grandoreiro and Astaroth ship packed in AutoIt and frequently run language checks (Portuguese 🇵🇹 or Spanish 🇪🇸), documented for Mispadu, before detonating. Mapped techniques include T1566.002, T1189, T1204.004, T1059.010 and T1218.007.
- Collection: After the May 2025 Lumma disruption that seized about 2,300 domains, Vidar and StealC dominate Brazilian 🇧🇷 infostealer submissions, at 73% and 49% of 107 analyses. Lumma-labeled sessions hit the judicial notice page noticeofpleadings[.]net, so some are legacy samples with neutralized C2. The shared tell across stealers and bankers is AutoIt3.exe launching from an IExpress-generated directory such as %TEMP%\IXP000.TMP\.
- Control and exfil: Astaroth and other bankers use ngrok tunnels for C2 (1.tcp.us-cal-1.ngrok[.]io, T1572). Banker sessions also showed DoH lookups for charlie.stufftoread[.]com. Telegram Bot API sendMessage exfil (T1567) showed multiple distinct tokens in 50 analyses, with banking-sector submissions at 25%, consistent with webmail and cPanel phishing kits. Unauthorized ScreenConnect instances, including ones delivered through legitimate services like Power BI, give hands-on-keyboard access that blends in with IT support (T1219).
- Pivots: 13.222.157[.]107:8138 links Brazilian 🇧🇷 banker sessions to Grandoreiro with Run key persistence (T1547.001). 64.89.163[.]22 ties loader distribution to UOL webmail payment lures. 62.60.226[.]159 serves generic executables in a 29-analysis msiexec cluster where Grandoreiro, Phorpiex, ScreenConnect and StealC co-occur. The report reads that as pay-per-install loader activity at moderate confidence, since no public source links Phorpiex to Grandoreiro. Submission geography reflects where samples were uploaded, not confirmed victims.
- Scope caveats: Target sectors were not directly observed. The WhatsApp propagation module (a session touched web.whatsapp[.]com/status.json) and the reliablelifecure[.]com panel remain unverified.
Takeaway: hunt behavior first. Look for AutoIt3.exe running from %TEMP% or any path containing IXP0, non-browser processes contacting api.telegram[.]org, PowerShell, mshta or curl spawned alongside Explorer RunMRU entries (the ClickFix trail), CurrentVersion\Run entries on hosts with AutoIt activity, and ScreenConnect instances outside your tenant allowlist. If you run banker samples, set Portuguese 🇵🇹 or Spanish 🇪🇸 locales or the geofence will hide the behavior. Where you process Pix payments, correlate active RMM sessions with suspicious transactions. The report lists the indicators and the TI query strings, and suggests validating the IPs and the 169.58.124[.]0/24 range before blocking.

item.title: Patching vCenter Zero-Day Is Only Step One
item.description:
CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) is an authentication bypass in vCenter's VMware Directory Service, exploited as a zero-day since early September 2026 by suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE. Patching closes the door, but the stolen SAML signing key and AD data keep working.
- The flaw: CWE-288 in an RPC interface on TCP 2012. SRP login generates timestamp-based predictable identifiers, letting an attacker recover the session key and become administrator[@]vsphere.local with no password. From there they can copy data.mdb, which holds SSO accounts and the private key that signs SAML tokens. Fixed Nov. 19 in VMSA-2026-0009 and added to CISA KEV Nov. 20, with a Nov. 23 deadline for U.S. 🇺🇸 federal agencies. No workaround. It is a different bug from CVE-2026-59309, and Mandiant saw it used against a vCenter already patched for the July flaw. Fixed builds: 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, 8.0 U3m, VCF 5.2.5. vCenter 7.0 has no public fix, so restrict port 2012. Skip the GitHub "PoC" from Nov. 20, it describes the wrong advisory. item.title: From a CMS exploit to Global Administrator: an AI pentest console inside a South Korean university, with 91 tables exported and 1,331 passwords cracked
item.description:
An open ARTEX working directory documents an autonomous pentest agent's takeover of a South Korean 🇰🇷 university, from a 2019 CMS flaw to Microsoft 365 Global Administrator and 20 fabricated student accounts.
- Researchers pulled 6,035 files (1.16 GB) from 38.60.157[.]51 on 20 Nov. Entry was pre-auth code execution in XpressEngine, fixed in 1.11.6 in October 2019 (T1190). Look for module_srl or selected_widget containing ../ or ${, then act=dispWidgetInfo with query parameters named 0 and 1. A _cfg_ plus four hex web shell followed. Per the operator's report, SYSTEM came from rewriting a privileged app's log4net.config twice within seconds. Defender was disabled, LSASS was dumped (70.9 MB), and SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY were saved with reg save.
- Pivot: chisel reverse SOCKS tunnels, persisted as scheduled task X9137Chisel (SYSTEM, onstart); a separate task, nc673, ran commands as the interactive user for DPAPI unwrap. A modified MS17-010 exploit added a local admin named after the ARTEX intent number. Plaintext connection strings in a classic ASP include opened the academic database. A VBScript run on the campus web server exported 91 tables (297 MB). Separately, a library/e-book web app member table has 60 columns including both halves of the national resident registration number.
- Cracking: 13 hashcat runs on CPU recovered 1,331 of 10,155 hashes. Unsalted SHA-256 student SSO hashes and MySQL web app hashes fell to digit masks, and an eight-digit mask took 352 accounts in two seconds. Worse, the SSO accepted the stored 44-character hash as the password, so the staff table was a list of working logins.
- Cloud: a staff session reached an M365 bridge whose reset form never asks for the old password. The operator then used the ROPC password grant with the Office client ID d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c for a Global Administrator token valid from 18:47 UTC on 16 Nov, and exported the full directory within two hours. From 17 to 18 Nov, 20 licensed student-style accounts were created, and a new account whose display name translates as "M365 operations management" was made Global Administrator (T1098.003). The bulk script's header says "authorised assessments only"; no scope or contract exists in the files.
Takeaway: ARTEX leaks its task numbering onto victims, so hunt for local accounts, folders, files or tasks named i plus three or four digits, such as C:\i3811 or C:\i1027_add.txt. In Entra, search sign-ins with AuthenticationProtocol ropc and a success result, Global Administrator added to an account created in the prior 48 hours, and any one identity creating 10 or more users in an hour. Preserve web server access logs, the Entra sign-in and audit logs, and the hosts' scheduled tasks. Also check for certutil -decode of .b64 files built by repeated echo appends from a web worker process. The report includes the KQL queries, host and web log hunt patterns, and an IOC table with tool hashes.

item.title: PolySwarm Special Report: The Expanding Healthcare Threat Surface
item.description:
PolySwarm's 2026 healthcare report finds one thread across ransomware, espionage and supply-chain incidents: trusted access. Stolen credentials, vendor APIs, remote services and developer accounts did the work, often well before any encryptor ran.
- Ransomware stayed the loudest threat. A CISA, FBI and HHS advisory update says Medusa, a RaaS crew running double extortion, hit more than 500 victims as of April 2026. Its affiliates get in through phishing, initial access brokers, exposed remote services and newly disclosed vulnerabilities (exploited within 24 hours), then use living-off-the-land techniques and legitimate remote management software. UMMC's ransomware attack on Feb 19 closed about 35 clinics, and the intruder may have had access from Feb 11. Medusa claimed it, but UMMC did not confirm that. Cedar County Memorial's Meditech EHR was down from Aug 14 to Aug 28. Leak site tracking shows 869 healthcare victims in 2026: The Gentlemen 97, Qilin 78, Akira 19.
- n0n is an AI-assisted extortion operation that emerged in September. SOCRadar found an exposed staging server with 1,719 files and an OpenCode agent writing and revising attack scripts. It found no exploits or CVEs. Every documented intrusion with a known access path used weak, stolen, reused or exposed credentials: FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing, RDP and WinRM password sweeps, exposed AWS keys, hijacked hosting sessions, and SaaS and CI/CD secrets. After access, the operator created concealed admin accounts, set up proxy and SSH access, harvested browser credentials and session tokens, and collected email and incoming MFA codes. It has 363 leak site claims, 31 in healthcare, and listed at least 11 pharma and biotech firms on Nov 16. PolySwarm says the 16 n0n toolkit files it holds are flagged by no engine, while 95 to 97% of Akira, Qilin and INC executables are flagged by three or more.
- State activity targeted research and infrastructure. UNC6508, a China-nexus cluster, compromised internet-facing REDCap installs, dropped a help.php web shell, then deployed INFINITERED. This custom malware has a dropper that intercepts upgrades, a credential harvester and a backdoor. It modifies legitimate REDCap files and inserts itself into the upgrade process, so it survives upgrades, and hides captured logins in the application's session database. Over a year later the actor replayed credentials against an enterprise admin account and created a content compliance rule named "Patroit" that silently forwarded mail to an actor-controlled Gmail address. Russian 🇷🇺 FSB Center 16 scans for routers with legacy SNMP and default community strings, then pulls configs out via TFTP. It has also exploited CVE-2018-0171 and CVE-2008-4128. Stryker's March 11 disruption was claimed by Handala, linked by researchers to Iranian 🇮🇷 interests. Employees reported Intune remote wipes, which Stryker did not confirm. Unit 42 found a malicious file used to run commands and hide activity.
- Third-party identity was the pivot. Veradigm: credentials for a Veradigm API were stolen from a vendor's environment and used to download patient data. LHC Group: a suspected vishing victim's stolen credentials were used on a vendor platform between April 7 and April 15. COPC: vishing led to about 1.4 million people potentially affected. Quest: access via Quanum Lab Services Manager, with the cause undisclosed. Boston Scientific: entry through an external-facing network device. Miasma is a parallel risk, not a confirmed healthcare compromise. A GitHub account compromised through a malicious VS Code extension pushed 32 [@]redhatcloudservices npm packages on May 29, with more than 90 malicious versions per Microsoft. Valid provenance came from the legitimate GitHub Actions OIDC workflow. The payload stole GitHub and npm tokens, SSH keys, cloud and Vault secrets, and could scrape runner memory.
Takeaway: a successful login proves little here, so hunt for what the identity did. Review VPN and RDP/WinRM auth logs for credential-stuffing patterns, new or hidden admin accounts, and mail routing or content compliance rules that forward externally. Check REDCap for help.php and modified core files. Check routers for SNMP exposure and TFTP config transfers. Audit vendor API tokens, and for npm, check what ran at install time rather than trusting provenance. Do not rely on AV alone for attacker tooling. Sample hashes for Akira, Anubis, INC, Medusa, Miasma, Qilin and The Gentlemen are in the report's IOC section.

item.title: Scanning from Subnet 109.160.32.0/24, (Mon, Nov 23rd)
item.description:
159 IPs in a Romania 🇷🇴 based hosting /24 (109.160.32[.]0/24) hit DShield sensors since 5 Sept, mostly SSH. 152 logged in and ran one uname command; 69 sent a first packet with a TTL above 230.
SANS ISC's Guy Bruneau traced a steady scanning and SSH login campaign from a subnet assigned to BANATSYNC SRL (AS198364) in Timisoara, Romania 🇷🇴. It was still ongoing at the time of writing. Two separate DShield sensors saw it regularly, one with 127 unique IPs and the other with 134.
- Behavior on the honeypot: of 159 IPs, 152 logged in over SSH using standard usernames such as root, ubuntu and admin. Every session ran a single command, uname -s -v -n -r -m, then disconnected immediately. That is host fingerprinting with no follow-on activity in the sessions. Ports targeted included TCP/22, TCP/2222 and TCP/2323, and the actors sometimes succeeded only after multiple attempts.
- The TTL oddity: firewall logs showed TTLs mostly between 45 and 52, with a second cluster between 232 and 243. Packet captures tied that cluster to 69 IPs using a static IPID of 54321. For those hosts, the first packet of each burst carried a high TTL (230+), and every packet after it used a normal Linux-range TTL.
- Worked example: for 109.160.32[.]146 on 13 Nov 2026, tshark showed the initial SYN at TTL 239. After the sensor's SYN-ACK, the source's reset (0x0004) carried TTL 50, and everything that followed stayed at 50. The inbound pattern was SYN, SYN-ACK, RST across the 69 IPs. The report's references point to ZMap's source, but it does not spell out the cause, so treat it as an observed fingerprint, not a confirmed tool.
- Infrastructure picture: Shodan checks on a sample showed SSH as the only exposed service, running OpenSSH 10.2p1 on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (for example 109.160.32[.]34 and 109.160.32[.]200) or OpenSSH 9.6p1 on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (109.160.32[.]141, 109.160.32[.]147, 109.160.32[.]150). Others, such as 109.160.32[.]12, 109.160.32[.]66, 109.160.32[.]80 and 109.160.32[.]88, had nothing open. VirusTotal pages for four sampled IPs describe the same SSH brute-force and run-a-command-then-disconnect behavior.
- Why it matters: IP reputation and TTL baselines alone would have split this single actor set into two populations. Mixed TTLs inside one flow look like noise unless you compare packet one against the rest of the session.
Takeaway: if you run a honeypot or keep full packet captures, group by source and compare TTL of the first packet against later packets, then pivot on IPID 54321. In cowrie data, search for the single-command uname -s -v -n -r -m session followed by an instant disconnect from the same /24. The report includes the Kibana DSL queries, the ES|QL queries (CIDR match on 109.160.32[.]0/24 and network.ttl >= 230), and the tshark command with the fields used to verify low and high TTL.

The report includes the Kibana DSL queries, the ES|QL queries (CIDR match on 109.160.32[.]0/24 and network.ttl >= 230), and the tshark command with the fields used to verify low and high TTL.

item.title: Detections Digest #20261123
item.description:
Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) coverage landed across Splunk, CrowdStrike and delta-tradecraft repos, alongside ClickFix evasion and nginx webshell rules. 40 new and 27 updated rules, Nov 16 to 23, 2026.
- Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) got layered coverage. Splunk added four rules: Zeek HTTP traffic with malformed Base64 padding, JVM HotSpot Base64 argument exceptions, HTTP Base64 activity paired with JVM errors, and decoder crashes correlated with Sysmon for Linux child process creation and file writes. Query-Hub's CrowdStrike Falcon queries find hosts running Java with x86-64 AVX-512 VBMI support and inbound connections. delta-tradecraft covers vulnerable HotSpot and Azul Prime builds with the AVX-512 Base64 path enabled, container exit codes and crash signals, and fatal error logs (hs_err_pid*.log). It also flags Java server processes spawning shells or script engines.
- ClickFix tradecraft is covered at both execution and persistence. Splunk added rules for cmd.exe obfuscation with superscript characters and call/set routines, plus self-deletion, and for binaries in user-writable paths writing CurrentVersion Run keys. A KQL rule from benscha catches ClickFix, FileFix and TerminalFix command lines from Explorer Run prompts, Windows Terminal and browser file dialogs. Browser-side rules use PowerShell Script Block Logging (EventCode 4104) and Security EventCode 4663 for non-browser access to Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Brave cache paths (cache smuggling). Others flag NativeMessagingHosts registry persistence and native messaging hosts spawning children from user-writable paths.
- Web server intrusion on Linux: new KQL queries watch nginx, OpenResty, PHP-FPM and uWSGI workers spawning shells, scripting interpreters or network binaries. They walk process ancestry up to three levels and correlate drops in /tmp, /var/tmp and /dev/shm with later execution. Neo23x0/signature-base broadened PHP webshell YARA, pairing $_GET, $_POST or php://input with eval, exec, system or assert, and adding base64_decode and openssl_decrypt payload patterns plus loop-based decoders.
- Linux privilege abuse and tunneling: three Splunk rules tied to CVE-2026-123158 cover auditd shells with a TTY under system UIDs, a failed then successful SSH login for service accounts, and an accepted SSH login followed by root execution via doas within 10 minutes. Splunk also added a multi-platform ngrok rule (authtoken configs, TCP tunnels to RDP and SMB, Invoke-Ngrok) and expanded Cloudflared detections. Separately, Linux macros moved from sysmon to sysmon_linux, which fixes silent data gaps in compile-after-delivery and unshare privilege escalation rules.
- Other adds: a Neo23x0 YARA rule for public Ghostscript Upload2Shell PoCs (CVE-2026-125396) that matches font loading sequences meant to escape -dSAFER. A KQL query for Defender for Endpoint flags connections tied to the Optimizely supply-chain compromise. CAPEv2 got YARA for StormKitty, WorldWind, Prynt and AsyncRAT. Sublime added PDF lure rules for fake invoices, W9 forms and Teams Planner.
Takeaway: the digest lists the rules by repo and rule name; the rules and queries themselves are in those repos. For Java4Shell, the digest gives no confirmed exploitation, so treat crashes as a possible attempt, not proof. Preserve hs_err_pid*.log files and container exit codes before restarts overwrite them, and check whether the crashing JVM later spawned a child process. If you adapted Linux Sysmon rules, confirm they point at sysmon_linux.

item.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 Supply Chain Attack: How to Secure AI Gateways Beyond Code Signatures
item.description:
LiteLLM's own release pipeline built, signed, and published 1.107.0 from an attacker-controlled lookalike fork on October 21, 2026. The source tag on GitHub was clean and the images carried a valid signature, so a signature check alone would have passed.
- Affected artifacts: all seven litellm==1.107.0 PyPI wheels (11:39 to 13:23 UTC), plus GHCR images (11:46 to 13:51) and Docker Hub images (11:46 to 14:20). The images sit behind the tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable for litellm, litellm-database, and litellm-non_root. The source distribution had a tampered build configuration but not the payload files. Mirrors, caches, and downstream images can extend exposure past these windows, so match digests rather than tags.
- Execution does not need an import. The wheels dropped cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py into site-packages, outside the litellm package. Python processes these at interpreter startup, so any Python launch in the environment, even an unrelated pip install, could run the credential collector. A separate loader could pull more code from an attacker-controlled server. On hosts, look for those startup files and a detached Python process holding /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock. A missing artifact does not prove a host is clean.
- How the pipeline fell: a config file with a key for LiteLLM's internal Agent Platform was committed to a public repository in May and never revoked. On October 10 the attacker used it to get an organization owner's GitHub CLI token, then harvested more maintainer tokens through short-lived workflows. On release day the owner token overrode branch protection and pointed the staging build at the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm fork, and a second stolen token approved production. This is separate from the March compromise of 1.82.7 and 1.82.8.
- Credential use was fast. Public research saw AWS instance-role credentials taken from CI runners and Kubernetes nodes validated with sts:GetCallerIdentity, then used to list Amazon Bedrock models the same day. What was at risk depends on where it ran. A gateway can hold provider keys, the proxy master key, virtual keys, and database credentials. A laptop or CI runner exposes source-control tokens, registry and deployment access, and sometimes signing material.
- Why signing failed: a signature proves who signed, not what source was built. Public analysis of the image provenance showed the real LiteLLM release workflow as builder and the lookalike fork as source repository. A policy that checked source repo and revision as well as the signature had what it needed to reject the release. LiteLLM rotated its signing key on October 23 and moved to keyless signing from v1.111.0-dev.3 on November 15. Keyless releases should be verified by certificate identity and OIDC issuer, not by key.
Response order: find every copy that ran, including transitive dependencies, lock files, build logs, CI runners, private mirrors, and image caches. Isolate and preserve filesystem, process, network, and identity evidence, and inspect from a known-clean system, since running Python or pip inside a suspect environment can trigger the payload again. Rotate from a clean machine, starting with credentials that mint tokens or change production, then review cloud, identity, model-provider, and source-control logs for use after exposure, including GetCallerIdentity from workload roles. Uninstalling the package is not recovery. Rebuild from a verified release, rebuild downstream images, confirm running digests, and keep watching the exposed identities after the workload is gone.
Takeaway: check base image digests and installed packages in every image, not build dates, since post-window builds that pulled from a cache or mirror can carry the payload. Pin approved digests and package hashes, and enforce source repo and revision from provenance in deployment policy.

item.title: Holiday Lures, Real Threats: 5 Thanksgiving and Black Friday Campaigns from 2026
item.description:
Five Thanksgiving and Black Friday lures, from Google Workspace phishing to a ScreenConnect e-card and a Word coupon dropping VBS, show why post-click behavior matters more than the email.
- Potluck phishing (Nov 4-5, US 🇺🇸 real estate network): "RSVP to Thanksgiving Potluck" came from a franchise office's front desk mailbox. "View & RSVP" led to trident-ww[.]com/ok/, a fake Cloudflare-style check, then a Google Workspace login in an iframe from om.anthonnyfry[.]com (path /gmail-login?sid=). Credentials were POSTed to /st and /e. Opening the form directly redirected elsewhere, which frustrates inspection. The operation has run since August 2026, with about 350 sandbox sessions and more than 170 domains. No malware was observed.
- E-card to ScreenConnect (Oct 30): Invitation RSVP.pdf with Blue Mountain branding linked to DocSend, then an HTML page in a public Cloudflare R2 bucket. It auto-downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from nepaldentalhome1.screenconnect[.]com (135.148.5[.]91). The page also looked up the visitor's IP via ipwho[.]is and ipify and sent it to a Telegram bot with sendMessage. The PDF isn't malicious by itself, and the installer is legitimate software. Post-install attacker actions were not confirmed.
- Fake MyChart survey (Nov 3-17): An image-only email, subject "Tell us about your MyChart experience", clicked through a traffic distribution system (TDS) with a fake slide-to-verify page, an eight-question survey, and a request for a $10.55 "processing fee" plus name, email, phone, and address. Shared offer ID 21058 in the image path and TDS parameters tied it to a wider promo operation. Card harvesting was not observed. Infrastructure includes ni03hfph[.]com, trustedaftermark[.]com, naverio[.]boats, and commercialbuygroup[.]com/medicarekit/.
- NDA phishing hidden in a real newsletter (Nov 6-10, 29 related tasks, small US 🇺🇸 businesses): A fake NDA "OPEN DOCUMENT" button sat above a genuine Black Friday newsletter with 30 to 46 links, one or two malicious. Mail went through Amazon SES from clinic-related domains and passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. The button hit compromised sites (addictionmiddletown[.]com/dashboard/, pakagrico[.]com/FRIS/), where FingerprintJS gated routing. Sandbox sessions only saw decoys like USA 🇺🇸 Today and SpaceX. The final phishing page was never seen.
- Word coupon with embedded VBS (Sep 14-Oct 5, nine tasks): "Click to get Coupon Code" hid an OLE package, Voucer.vbs, with no macros. The user had to open it and click through an Office warning. The chain was WINWORD.EXE to wscript.exe to schtasks.exe. It tried to fetch hxxps://forum.cryptopia[.]gdn/sys.exe to %APPDATA%\sys.exe and create a task named Cclenears that runs every three hours. The download failed in all nine tasks, so the payload family is unknown. All runs were Windows 7 with Word 2010, which may mean campaign testing.
Takeaway: Hunt for WINWORD.EXE spawning wscript.exe, wscript.exe spawning schtasks.exe, a Cclenears scheduled task, and %APPDATA%\sys.exe. Flag new ScreenConnect MSI installs that arrive straight from a browser download. For phishing, pivot on shared redirect patterns, credential POST paths, and identifiers like offer ID 21058. Treat a failed payload fetch as an attempt, not a clean bill of health. Hashes and further IOCs are in the report.

item.title: Threat Researcher’s Notebook: SSO Vishing Campaign Associated with Emerging “Inception” Extortion Group
item.description:
A new extortion crew calling itself Inception has claimed seven United States 🇺🇸 victims, and ReversingLabs ties the claims to an SSO vishing campaign running since late October 2026. The lures are web-only, legal-themed domains that send non-targets to the real Okta or NetIQ login.
The leak site went public on November 17, 2026 (incptbug3ziqym4rhgsj7h7hbpzt3v4ympcf42gsdb5haqq237fziaad[.]onion) with AMD, Cigna Healthcare, Henry Schein, Paychex and PepsiCo. AutoZone followed on November 19 and Lucid Motors on November 21. These are unverified adversary claims, not confirmed breaches.
- Delivery is by phone, not email. None of the lure domains have MX, DKIM, DMARC or any mail DNS, so the operators skip email controls and walk targets to lookalike SSO pages. Naming is a single brand paired with legal terms: legal-amd[.]com, legal-pepsico[.]com, legal-paychex[.]com, legal-henryschein[.]com, legal-lucidmotors[.]com, legal-vrtx[.]com, legal-twitch[.]tv, plus paramount[.]legal and wynnresorts[.]legal.
- The kit filters visitors. Unwanted traffic is forwarded to the victim's real Okta tenant, such as amd.okta[.]com or pepsico.okta[.]com. legal-vrtx[.]com loaded the Okta sign-in widget directly, and legal-lucidmotors[.]com pointed at a NetIQ and OpenText Access Manager path. The operators research each target's SSO platform and adapt the kit. Nine staged domains, including ones mimicking Starbucks, Ulta, Paramount, Nintendo and Jones Day, forward to the brand's benign corporate site.
- The infrastructure fingerprint is consistent. Domains are registered between 18:00 and 00:59 UTC, with a cluster in the 19:00 hour, and most go through NICENIC with WHOIS registrant location pairs of North Carolina, Chile 🇨🇱 and Bermuda. They move to Cloudflare within minutes across fifteen nameserver pairs, likely one account. The malavika/pedro pair hosted the Cigna and Henry Schein lures alongside Duolingo, Morningstar, Western Union, Dropbox, Indeed and Vertex. Many domains were later parked on registrar defaults or suspended.
- Multi-registrar batching links the accounts. legal-henryschein[.]com was registered at NICENIC at 19:28 UTC on November 8, 2026, and henryschein-legal[.]com followed thirteen minutes later at Spaceship. Smaller setups used NameSilo with an Arizona profile, Spaceship with a Delaware profile, and Tucows with Njalla privacy for legal-creditkarma[.]com.
- Scope goes beyond the leak site. The report describes twenty-one confirmed domains with direct SSO kit evidence, forty-one more attributed with high confidence, and four at medium confidence. Shared pivots point to dozens of corporate targets not yet listed, so your org may be staged before any claim appears.
Takeaway: Hunt DNS, proxy and identity provider logs from October 21, 2026 onward for lookups to the report's domain list, cross-origin SSO referrers, and anomalous post-authentication activity. If targeting is confirmed, revoke active sessions and reset credentials. Watch new-domain and certificate transparency feeds for brand-plus-legal names registered in the evening UTC window. Have help desks require strict identity verification before any credential or MFA reset, and alert on unexpected MFA changes. The full domain IOC list is in the report.

item.title: 99 IPs but a C2 ain’t one: An Active Intrusion Campaign Against Check Point Security Management Servers
item.description:
GreyNoise tracks GT13, a suspected AI-enabled campaign against Check Point Security Management Servers, hitting at least 22 orgs worldwide and using a compromised HFS server as a relay.
- Scope: confirmed attack activity ran Oct 17 to Nov 2, 2026, across financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. GreyNoise does not attribute GT13 to any tracked group or assess motive. The actor used 99 IPs, all ExpressVPN egress or compromised Check Point devices, over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files. The actor already had Check Point access before the HFS compromise, and how they got it is unknown. Persistent access suggests the campaign is ongoing.
- Relay build: on 2026-10-02 the actor hit Rejetto HFS with CVE-2026-61500. Repeated POSTs to loginSrp1 leaked sid values from Math.random(), enough to rebuild V8 PRNG state, recover the cookie signing key, and forge an admin session. The forged cookie carried allow_session_ip_change:true, so it worked from any VPN exit. The actor then used HFS middleware hooks to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. A check-in ran "uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami". An attempted ZULT Linux implant download via server_code from newpayapp[.]com (registered 2026-03-13) failed. The actor came back over SSH the next day.
- Hop tradecraft: a script at /root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py stood up an unauthenticated HTTP server for uploads. The actor installed Nmap and Chisel, ran a Chisel server as a reverse proxy, and ran Chisel in client mode on a Victim A asset. Bulk results from 24 compromised Check Point servers landed in /root/exfil/pc_<victim IP>.txt. Each server pushed its file via scp, so each holds the SSH private key matching the key planted on the hop.
- Check Point abuse: the actor used exploit[.]py, a purported adaptation of the Metasploit module for CVE-2026-16232 (SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), to launch over 100 management tasks. These copied the firewall database and Internal CA, minted a certificate (pivot.p12), and unloaded security policies, which would disable the firewall. pull_<id>.py chained exploit_socks.py to harvest credentials, CA files, and firewall config through one compromised device to the hop. One error output showed a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant.
- Internal ops: the actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko, and at least 30 Python scripts, including spray_portal.py, comb[.]py, ssh_comb.py, and ssh_spray.py with victim-themed passwords. Exploit attempts hit Netlogon CVE-2020-1472, Citrix CVE-2023-4966, Ivanti CVE-2024-21893, Exchange CVE-2021-26855/34473, and vCenter CVE-2021-21972/CVE-2023-34048. On 2026-11-02 the actor even tried to patch its own hop for CVE-2026-98432 with nftables rules dropping IPv4 packets with IP options, to keep rivals out.
Takeaway: on Check Point management servers, check /etc/ld.so.preload and /usr/lib/.libproc.so, review Run Script and management task history for bulk certificate or policy-unload actions, and look for pivot.p12, unexpected SSH private keys, and scp uploads to unknown hosts. On any HFS host, hunt for loginSrp1 POST bursts, forged-cookie admin requests, command hooks, unexpected authorized_keys entries, and /root/exfil. Preserve the nftables rules too. The report has excerpts of the actor's scripts but no IOC table.

item.title: KQL of the Week: Hunting Exposed Offensive AI Infrastructure with KQL Queries
item.description:
Detect FYI shows how to hunt for exposed offensive AI infrastructure in Defender XDR. It pulls the offensive[.]agency feeds, built on ONYPHE scan data, straight into KQL with externaldata(). The point is to explain why endpoints talk to these hosts, not to flag every match.
Some AI-powered offensive security frameworks now expose web consoles and APIs on the public Internet. offensive[.]agency tracks them passively, using web page, favicon, and certificate fingerprints to mark probable or confirmed deployments. An exposed agent is not automatically malicious, since researchers, pentesters, students, and criminals all run these tools. That makes every match a triage question.
- Hunt 1, outbound: The report loads the IP export with externaldata(), strips comment lines, and joins on RemoteIP in DeviceNetworkEvents (last 7 days, ActionType ConnectionSuccess). The same IP join runs against UrlClickEvents using the IPAddress field. CDN and shared hosting such as Cloudflare will produce false positives, so an IP match alone proves nothing.
- Hunt 2, domains: Because IPs behind CDNs are unreliable, the report matches on hostname instead. It parses Host out of RemoteUrl in DeviceNetworkEvents and out of Url in UrlClickEvents, lowercases it, and joins against the domain export. This helps when several unrelated services share one IP, and it does not depend on DNS events being collected.
- Hunt 3, inbound: Same IP list, but filtered to ActionType startswith "Inbound". The projection keeps Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType, and InitiatingProcessFileName. The report calls out unexpected inbound connections to administrative services, repeated attempts, and one external IP touching multiple internal servers.
- Hunt 4, C2 co-hosting: The c2=1 filter returns infrastructure where other services, including command-and-control frameworks, have also been observed. The query summarizes per DeviceName and RemoteIP: first and last seen, connection count, and sets of initiating processes, ports, remote URLs, and action types. The report is explicit that a hit does not mean the connection used a C2 protocol, because the same IP may host unrelated services.
- Evidence caveats: The tracker is passive and never touches the hosts. scope=all includes historical observations, and an IP seen in the past may now belong to someone else, so check matches against the observation dates in the source data. externaldata() fetches the feed at execution time, so results can change between runs.
DFIR takeaway: treat these as triage leads, not verdicts. For any hit, pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName, the ports, and the user context to decide whether it is a sanctioned red team or an unknown process beaconing out. Inbound hits against admin services deserve the fastest look. For reproducible casework, save a copy of the feed and note the collection time with your findings, so you can later show which list produced which match. Full KQL for all four hunts is in the report.
