item.title: Agentic Attacks: In The Wild
item.description:
Agentic offensive frameworks like ARTEX are driving a surge in cloud intrusions. Wiz Research paired its telemetry with an operator's leaked logs and found noisy, machine-speed attacks that label their own work.
- Scope: ARTEX is open source with hundreds of forks, and others like Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike are in the wild too. "ARTEX" activity comes from unrelated operators, so it is not one campaign or actor. Since the Black October post, vendors have disclosed about twenty more related incidents, and Wiz's CIRT reports 3x the engagement requests.
- ARTEX-Harvester: tied at varying confidence to more than a dozen organizations between late October and mid-November 2026, clustered by a distinctive boto3 build, cross-victim incrementing Intent IDs and proxy pool overlap. Nearly every request came from a different residential or ISP exit, over 220 IPs at a single target, so IP blocking does little. The operator tried stolen creds, anonymous storage, sign-up and password-reset abuse, and identity-provider probing in parallel.
- One success chain: stolen VCS credentials opened private repos. The attacker created branches that abused CI workload identity trust, and harvest workflows dumped secrets and Terraform state. Separately, a stolen service-account token from an app pod could create privileged pods with the node root filesystem mounted. A "node-level collector" pod grabbed the kubelet PKI and every projected service-account token. The cert-manager token could read ArgoCD secrets, which led to cluster-admin.
- Both sides of one intrusion: an operator's open directory (over 3,000 files) matched the victim telemetry. Over four days in October the attacker hit two AWS accounts and seven EKS clusters. The chain ran from a stolen Terraform-runner session to a privileged pod and cluster-admin binding, then Jenkins RCE with a reverse shell. A pod escape dropped an ld[.]so.preload userland rootkit with a DNS-tunnel channel, disguised as a fontconfig service, with zero VirusTotal detections. Node, IRSA and Terraform-runner credentials were then used from the attacker's own server to read Terraform state and Secrets Manager and open SSM sessions.
- What the logs showed beyond telemetry: forged IdP admin tokens exposed 3,392 users and live sessions, beacons went to 19 hosts, and 50 SSH keys were pulled from a bastion database. The production Jenkinsfile was modified to run before its approval gate. CyberStrikeAI drove it, with csai- on nearly everything created (csai-escape pods, a csai-pentest-role IAM role, a csai-probe runner). Anthropic API keys were harvested from 50 hosts, and AI coding-assistant session histories were mined for SSO credentials. Separately, Censys counted over 1,400 exposed ARTEX consoles in early November.
- Self-labeling is the tell: pentest-recon user agents, pentest-* workspaces and pods, and a task counter like pentest-iNNNNNN. In-cluster, look for privileged container creation, nsenter, IMDS kube-env queries and drifted scripts reaching for cloud credentials. The report notes its rules are perishable as tools get renamed.
Takeaway: hunt your cloud audit logs and Kubernetes pod and workspace names for pentest-, csai- and the iNNNNNN counter. Check nodes for ld[.]so.preload entries and fontconfig lookalike services. Alert on EC2 or ECS task credentials used outside AWS, unusual GetCallerIdentity and mass secret value retrieval. Review CI branches that touch workload identity trust. Attacker IPs (for example the ARTEX operator hosts 68.68.250[.]114, 192.238.246[.]157 and 104.207.150[.]173) are in the report, and a CSV is in the wiz-research-iocs repository. The report lists the detection rule names too.

item.title: Supply Chain Compromise Backdoors Six WP connect Plugins, Blocked by WordPress.org’s Release Hold
item.description:
Backdoored releases of six WP connect WordPress plugins were committed from the developer's own account, but WordPress[.]org's release hold kept them from sites. CVE-2026-135202, CVSS 9.8, unpatched.
- Scope: on November 22, 2026, over roughly two hours, new releases hit Air WP Sync 2.9.1 to 2.9.4, WP Sync for Notion 1.7.4, Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms 2.6.3, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable 2.5.4, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion 1.6.4, and Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce 1.0.2. The plugins have an estimated 3,600+ active installs. Each release added includes/airwp-online.php and a require_once line in the main plugin file. The release before each one is clean. The pattern points to a compromised developer account, and the developer reports one, though details are pending.
- Backdoor mechanics: the module poses as an "Online module (Analytics & Auto-Update)" but hardcodes its endpoint to tascredit-pay[.]com/api, with /sync appended. It runs on the init hook on every request, including unauthenticated page views, plus a half-hourly WP-Cron fallback. It POSTs the site URL, PHP, WordPress and OS versions, the PHP user, and prior command output, with TLS verification disabled. The server's code field is base64-decoded, optionally XOR-decrypted, and run through eval(). The server can also rewrite its own api_url and check-in interval to move infrastructure.
- Command set: queued commands dispatch to act_ methods. sh runs OS commands, file reads, writes or deletes files, db dumps tables, and dump_wp_users returns logins, emails and password hashes. webshell drops a standalone PHP shell that keeps working after the plugin is removed. persist registers an hourly WP-Cron hook that evals attacker code.
- Why it stalled: WordPress[.]org's Protect The Shire cooling-off delay held the releases, and its automated reviewer Gandalf independently detected the code and halted them. All six plugins were closed that evening, and the backdoored versions were never released to sites. Before that change, auto-updating sites would have pulled a 4:30 PM release on their next check. Wordfence's PRISM flagged the module by diffing releases, and Computeronfire independently reported the Air WP Sync backdoor.
- Artifacts to check: wp-content/plugins/<plugin>/includes/airwp-online.php. Outbound traffic to tascredit-pay[.]com, or the user agent AirWP-Sync/… (compatible; like GoogleBot). wp_options rows starting with airwp_, including airwp_client_id, airwp_api_url, airwp_pending_cmd, airwp_pending_report, airwp_capture_url, airwp_interval and airwp_last_run. WP-Cron events airwp_tick or airwp_persist_tick, or any unfamiliar hourly hook. Unexpected PHP files in wp-content/uploads/.
Takeaway: no exploitation of sites is reported, since the versions never shipped. Still, inventory your plugin versions against the list above. If one is present, preserve first: export the airwp_ options (airwp_pending_report holds the last command and result), the cron option in wp_options, and any uploads PHP files, then remove the plugin. Removal alone is not enough, because webshells and cron persistence outlive it. Treat the site as compromised, rotate admin passwords and secret keys, and run a full malware scan. IOCs are in the report.

item.title: ARTEX leads to persistent ZQAgent backdoor
item.description:
NVISO saw the LLM-driven intrusion tool ARTEX deploy ZQAgent, a new Linux backdoor that gives the operator a long-lasting foothold. That breaks the usual smash-and-grab pattern, where isolating initial access and revoking credentials was enough to contain these intrusions.
- Who and where: ZQAgent is named after ARTEX artifacts. NVISO saw it in Belgium 🇧🇪, first staged as /tmp/zqa/systemd-timesyncd, and similar samples were reported from Taiwan 🇹🇼. All known samples use 37.122.150[.]15 and bloonspace[.]com for C2, which NVISO associates with FOG0003. Team Cymru network intelligence suggests FOG0003 deployed it within Asia against government and human-rights organizations. NVISO believes the persistent backdoor comes from operator-specific instructions, not the tool acting autonomously.
- Runtime evasion: ZQAgent copies itself into a temporary anonymous memory file, which shows up as the apparent filename /memfd:a (deleted). It then restarts as a detached process impersonating dbus-daemon with this spoofed command line: /usr/bin/dbus-daemon --session --address=systemd: --nofork --nopidfile --systemd-activation --syslog-only. The spoofed process is not linked to the original executable. Configuration is encrypted dynamically and only decrypted briefly when evaluated, and network traffic uses multiple encryption layers, including ChaCha20 variants.
- Capabilities: arbitrary command execution through /bin/sh -c (0x2B), memory-only memfd managed processes (0x34), and managed interactive shells using /bin/bash or /bin/sh (0x47, 0x48). It also offers file move, rename, delete and directory listing, process listing and termination, and blocking and non-blocking TCP/UDP connection management for tunneling. Opcode 0x1C lets the operator enable, disable or check persistence.
- Persistence: it uses both systemd services and cron, and time-stomps every staged artifact. The binary lands under an attacker-chosen name in /usr/lib/systemd/ for root, ~/.local/share/ for other users, or /tmp/.local/share/ if HOME is unset. The unit file goes to /etc/systemd/system/NAME.service for root, or ~/.config/systemd/user/NAME.service otherwise (or /tmp/.config/systemd/user/ if HOME is unset). The unit is described as "Device event journal daemon" with Restart=always, RestartSec=30, and StandardOutput and StandardError set to null. Root units use multi-user[.]target, non-root units use default[.]target and systemctl --user, and non-root sessions call loginctl enable-linger to outlive logouts. The cron side drops /etc/cron.d/NAME for root with "[@]reboot root BINARY >/dev/null 2>&1", while non-root sessions append to the user's crontab through the crontab binary.
- Why it matters: NVISO warns that LLM-driven tooling will likely spread to ransomware, where it could cut time-to-ransom from hours to minutes, and to espionage, where it could widen scope. Its advice is hardened perimeters, segmentation, mandatory asset security telemetry and much faster response, including automated asset isolation.
Takeaway: do not trust timestamps here, since artifacts are time-stomped. Hunt on content and process state. Look for running processes with the spoofed dbus-daemon command line whose binary shows as /memfd:a (deleted), unit files with the description "Device event journal daemon" in the paths above, [@]reboot entries in /etc/cron.d or user crontabs that redirect to /dev/null, and unexpected loginctl enable-linger on non-root accounts. Capture memory before killing the process, because the running image lives only in an anonymous memory file. Also block and search for 37.122.150[.]15 and bloonspace[.]com.
Sample SHA256: c5d1358ece7dff7834507a29f59fdc35a1a2afa3045ae8d754fb497f6f999296. Full IOC table, public sample hashes and YARA rules for the backdoor, its persistence service and its cron job are in NVISO's report.

item.content:encoded:
NVISO saw the LLM-driven intrusion tool ARTEX deploy ZQAgent, a new Linux backdoor that gives the operator a long-lasting foothold. That breaks the usual smash-and-grab pattern, where isolating initial access and revoking credentials was enough to contain these intrusions.

- Who and where: ZQAgent is named after ARTEX artifacts. NVISO saw it in Belgium 🇧🇪, first staged as /tmp/zqa/systemd-timesyncd, and similar samples were reported from Taiwan 🇹🇼. All known samples use 37.122.150[.]15 and bloonspace[.]com for C2, which NVISO associates with FOG0003. Team Cymru network intelligence suggests FOG0003 deployed it within Asia against government and human-rights organizations. NVISO believes the persistent backdoor comes from operator-specific instructions, not the tool acting autonomously.

- Runtime evasion: ZQAgent copies itself into a temporary anonymous memory file, which shows up as the apparent filename /memfd:a (deleted). It then restarts as a detached process impersonating dbus-daemon with this spoofed command line: /usr/bin/dbus-daemon --session --address=systemd: --nofork --nopidfile --systemd-activation --syslog-only. The spoofed process is not linked to the original executable. Configuration is encrypted dynamically and only decrypted briefly when evaluated, and network traffic uses multiple encryption layers, including ChaCha20 variants.

- Capabilities: arbitrary command execution through /bin/sh -c (0x2B), memory-only memfd managed processes (0x34), and managed interactive shells using /bin/bash or /bin/sh (0x47, 0x48). It also offers file move, rename, delete and directory listing, process listing and termination, and blocking and non-blocking TCP/UDP connection management for tunneling. Opcode 0x1C lets the operator enable, disable or check persistence.

- Persistence: it uses both systemd services and cron, and time-stomps every staged artifact. The binary lands under an attacker-chosen name in /usr/lib/systemd/ for root, ~/.local/share/ for other users, or /tmp/.local/share/ if HOME is unset. The unit file goes to /etc/systemd/system/NAME.service for root, or ~/.config/systemd/user/NAME.service otherwise (or /tmp/.config/systemd/user/ if HOME is unset). The unit is described as "Device event journal daemon" with Restart=always, RestartSec=30, and StandardOutput and StandardError set to null. Root units use multi-user[.]target, non-root units use default[.]target and systemctl --user, and non-root sessions call loginctl enable-linger to outlive logouts. The cron side drops /etc/cron.d/NAME for root with "[@]reboot root BINARY >/dev/null 2>&1", while non-root sessions append to the user's crontab through the crontab binary.

- Why it matters: NVISO warns that LLM-driven tooling will likely spread to ransomware, where it could cut time-to-ransom from hours to minutes, and to espionage, where it could widen scope. Its advice is hardened perimeters, segmentation, mandatory asset security telemetry and much faster response, including automated asset isolation.

Takeaway: do not trust timestamps here, since artifacts are time-stomped. Hunt on content and process state. Look for running processes with the spoofed dbus-daemon command line whose binary shows as /memfd:a (deleted), unit files with the description "Device event journal daemon" in the paths above, [@]reboot entries in /etc/cron.d or user crontabs that redirect to /dev/null, and unexpected loginctl enable-linger on non-root accounts. Capture memory before killing the process, because the running image lives only in an anonymous memory file. Also block and search for 37.122.150[.]15 and bloonspace[.]com.

Sample SHA256: c5d1358ece7dff7834507a29f59fdc35a1a2afa3045ae8d754fb497f6f999296. Full IOC table, public sample hashes and YARA rules for the backdoor, its persistence service and its cron job are in NVISO's report.

item.title: ARTEX führt zu einer dauerhaften ZQAgent-Backdoor
item.description:
NVISO saw LLM-driven tool ARTEX drop ZQAgent, a persistent Linux backdoor, in an incident in Belgium 🇧🇪. Smash-and-grab AI attacks rarely leave persistence, so this is a shift. The C2 infrastructure is tied to FOG0003.
NVISO's report says LLM-assisted intrusions have mostly followed one pattern: exploit a vulnerability or abuse credentials, move fast, stash credentials for later, and leave little else. Containing them usually means isolating the initial access vector and resetting every compromised or stored credential. ZQAgent breaks that pattern. NVISO suspects the backdoor was a specific operator instruction rather than the tool's autonomous behavior.
- Who and where: ZQAgent is named after artifacts found in ARTEX. NVISO found it in Belgium 🇧🇪 at /tmp/zqa/systemd-timesyncd, and similar samples were reported from Taiwan 🇹🇼. All known samples are configured for C2 at 37.122.150[.]15 and bloonspace[.]com, which NVISO attributes to FOG0003. Team Cymru network data suggests FOG0003 likely used ZQAgent in Asia too, apparently against government bodies and human rights organizations.
- Runtime evasion: ZQAgent copies itself into a temporary anonymous in-memory file, so the process shows as /memfd:a (deleted). It then restarts as an independent process and rewrites its command line to pose as the dbus-daemon utility: /usr/bin/dbus-daemon --session --address=systemd: --nofork --nopidfile --systemd-activation --syslog-only. Config is encrypted dynamically and decrypted only briefly for use, and network traffic is wrapped in multiple encryption layers, including ChaCha20 variants.
- Capabilities: arbitrary code execution, filesystem operations, and network tunneling. Opcode 0x1C enables, disables, or checks persistence. 0x2B runs a command via /bin/sh -c as a managed process. 0x34 creates a memory-only managed process via memfd. 0x47 starts a managed shell, /bin/bash or /bin/sh as fallback. The report's opcode table also covers file moves, directory listing, process kill, and TCP/UDP connection handling.
- Persistence, two mechanisms plus timestomping of every dropped artifact. As root, the binary is copied under an attacker-chosen name to /usr/lib/systemd/%s with a unit at /etc/systemd/system/%s.service. As another user it goes to ~/.local/share/%s with a unit at ~/.config/systemd/user/%s.service. If HOME is unset, it falls back to /tmp/.local/share/%s and /tmp/.config/systemd/user/%s.service. The unit's Description is "Device event journal daemon", with Restart=always, RestartSec=30, and output sent to null. It is enabled via systemctl (with --user when not root), and non-root runs use loginctl enable-linger to survive logoff. The cron path writes an [@]reboot root entry to /etc/cron.d/%s as root, or appends to the user's crontab otherwise.
- Why it matters: NVISO warns that LLMs could cut time-to-ransom from hours to minutes and widen espionage reach. It argues for hardening exposed systems, mandatory security telemetry, shorter response times, and revisiting automated asset isolation.
Takeaway: because timestamps are manipulated, don't trust file times. Hunt on content and behavior instead. Look for processes running as /memfd:a (deleted) while posing as dbus-daemon, for systemd units described as "Device event journal daemon", and for [@]reboot cron entries in /etc/cron.d or user crontabs. Block and search for 37.122.150[.]15 and bloonspace[.]com. One ZQAgent SHA256 is c5d1358ece7dff7834507a29f59fdc35a1a2afa3045ae8d754fb497f6f999296. The full hash set (SHA256, SHA1, MD5) and YARA rules for the backdoor, the persistence service, and the cron job are in NVISO's report. After isolating the entry point, reset stored credentials and remove the persistence artifacts.

item.title: Hunting EvilTokens: residual activity after takedown
item.description:
EvilTokens, the phishing-as-a-service kit that hijacks Microsoft 365 through the OAuth device-code flow, is still producing new infrastructure after Microsoft's September 22 takedown. Microsoft tracks its developer and support operator as Storm-2992, and the kit was linked to 12,000+ compromised inboxes across 10,000+ organizations. Two men were arrested in the UK 🇬🇧 eleven days before the takedown.
- How it works: the lure (Adobe, DocuSign or SharePoint themed) shows a real device code and sends the victim to the genuine microsoft[.]com/devicelogin page, so "check the URL" fails. The backend polls Microsoft's token endpoint and ends up holding an access token and a refresh token (T1528, T1550.001). The lure also copies the code to the clipboard. The report's lead indicator is secure-link-c96a.amcobisolutions.workers[.]dev/share/CPTq-Xg99BM, seen August 25, 2026.
- Hunting the backend: the kit's calls to /api/device/start and the /status/<uuid> poll are searchable in urlscan. Titles alone are not selective, so a host only counts if urlscan shows both the landing page and the /api/device/start call. A second pivot is the non-standard CORS header X-Antibot-Token (alongside X-Page-Id and X-Cookie-Mode), searched in FOFA and then confirmed against a devicelogin link in VirusTotal.
- After the takedown: new hosts kept appearing, many on Bunny CDN, while the device-code calls still route to a Workers[.]dev host behind the scenes. Some legitimate domains appear to be compromised and repurposed to serve the kit. Naming patterns decay (the -s-account pattern dropped by half between March and April), but the device-login calls, the status poll and the clipboard write are behavioral and harder to change. A lure scanned on October 28, 2026 was still generating live device codes.
- Cluster 1, shared __DESTINATION_URL: four hosts point to the same e-signing link, app1.leegality[.]com/sign/a53e553f-c8ed-425e-a6ed-1f5389eee235. The lures are Microsoft and OneDrive sign-in pages with business-paperwork titles, and most hostnames contain portail. First seen October 21 to November 10. A separate set of hosts under yahoosign[.]com (for example cisco.yahoosign[.]com) appeared October 17 and 18, each prefixed with a company name.
- Cluster 2, throwaway mail accounts: Workers hostnames embed the registration e-mail domain plus the default -s-account suffix. Two disposable domains, dropoffs[.]org and dropons[.]com, each map to single-host accounts with hyphenated first-name-style local parts and xxxx-xxxx-xxxx Worker names, mostly serving a OneDrive "Shared Document" lure.
- AI angle: per Sekoia, the admin portal pulls mailbox, contacts and calendar via Microsoft Graph, then uses LLM stages to score BEC opportunities and draft BEC emails. Output goes to an attacker Telegram bot.
Takeaway: block device code flow in Entra ID Conditional Access (Conditions > Authentication Flows), running report-only first to find legitimate use. Where you cannot block, hunt Entra sign-in logs for Authentication Protocol: Device Code. In Sentinel: SigninLogs | where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode" | where ResultType == "0" | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, UserAgent, Location. Review any you did not set up on purpose. On a hit, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, remove any registered device (operators have registered one within 10 minutes of token theft), and disable the account rather than relying on a password reset. The full host list with first-seen dates is in the report's IOC section.

item.title: Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Hijack MSP Technician PCs Without Warning
item.description:
Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9) in ConnectWise ScreenConnect: a guest can push and run a file on an MSP technician's host with no prompt. Fixed in client 26.6.5.
- The flaw: a guest in a session can transfer a file to the technician's host and get the technician's own client to execute it. The technician sees no prompt and only has to join the session. That can be an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer session where the attacker slipped in as an extra guest. A technician workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, which is why it is the target.
- Observed chain (Huntress, Nov 12, 2026): a guest-pushed batch file, update_224ac089.bat, decoded a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID and registered the infection. It then pulled WindowsUpdate.msi from masterdarky[.]com and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointed at the attacker's relay. Total time was about 9 seconds.
- Scale and spray: between Oct 20 and Nov 16, 2026, Huntress saw at least 688,000 guest run-file requests for update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat against 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. Requests were repeated and came from guests with blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames. This is blind spraying, not tailored targeting.
- Canary and targeted cases: a guest at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a harmless marker.txt two seconds after a technician joined, apparently to confirm the exploit worked before sending the real payload. In an October 2026 targeted attack on an MSP, the attacker joined three real technician-created sessions as a guest and had the client run a file that dropped Sync.bat into the technician's Windows Startup folder for persistence.
- Related but separate activity: this is distinct from the SCKit wave, where an authentication flaw in a third-party extension gave access to partner ScreenConnect environments. Separately, as of Nov 13, Huntress saw 2,408 unauthorized guest sessions enrolled since Nov 3 across at least 118 self-hosted servers belonging to 109 protected organizations. Nearly all came from one IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106, through a scripted emulator using relay addresses taken from public Access installers. Guest machine names are exchange-themed, like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE. No file transfers or command execution followed, so these look like bait to get technicians to connect.
Takeaway: update technician host clients to 26.6.5 or later. If you cannot patch yet, remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups. Then hunt. In your ScreenConnect server's session and guest activity, look for run-file requests for update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat, blank or default Windows guest names, and files pushed seconds after a technician joins. On technician workstations, check the Startup folder for Sync.bat, look for WindowsUpdate.msi, and look for a ScreenConnect client pointing at a relay you do not recognize. Also check for traffic to masterdarky[.]com and Telegram bot calls. If you find a hit, isolate the workstation and rotate every credential reachable from it.

item.title: OXLoader abuses DLL hijacking to distribute different malware families
item.description:
OXLoader is now loading through DLL hijacking, using copyright-complaint ZIPs and fake activators from GitLab to deliver Remcos, OverLord, PureRAT, Lunex Stealer, LOLD, and Hermes. Malwarebytes reports a rise in activity, and the payload changes by campaign.
- Delivery and lures: Elastic first documented OXLoader in June 2026, with Google Ads pushing CASTLESTEALER. Malwarebytes now sees ZIPs posing as brand-IP complaints, reached through emailed PDFs or Google Sites pages, including Evidence_of_Violation.zip. WinWord.exe is renamed with double extensions like evidence_of_violation.docx.exe and sideloads a malicious msvcr100.dll. Some lures use long-named .bat files that pull a ZIP holding the malicious DLL. Fake activators and cracks on GitLab form a third route.
- Hijack chain: Abused hosts include Qt5Widgets.dll, Qt6Core.dll, SDL3.dll, UnityPlayer.dll, ANCUtility.dll, dbghelp.dll, msvcr100.dll, and WindowsCodecs.dll, paired with executables tied to Microsoft apps, Steam, OBS Studio, and PDF or Word readers. In the GitLab case, a legitimate Take-Two Interactive executable loads a trojanized UnityPlayer.dll. manifest.json holds encrypted shellcode that gets injected into another legitimate DLL. Shellcode on disk can also be named Dependencies.manifest or titles.png. Code is obfuscated with opaque predicates, control flow flattening, and mixed Boolean arithmetic. Malwarebytes traced it with the Sogen emulator.
- Evasion checks: The loader fails WNetAddConnection2W and WNetGetResourceParentW on purpose and looks for error 67 and 487 to spot VMs. It wants 3 or more processors and a display refresh rate of at least 20 Hz, read via powershell Get-WmiObject Win32_VideoController. It also checks GetUserGeoID against a list including Russia 🇷🇺, Belarus 🇧🇾, and Kazakhstan 🇰🇿, and the UI language against Russian 🇷🇺 (0x419). If it flags an analysis environment, it shuts the system down via cmd or jumps to an invalid address. Patching the function at 0x1807999c2 bypasses the checks.
- Persistence and staging: Files are copied to C:\ProgramData\{random 7 characters}\ as the renamed executable (fl studio pro.exe in this case), unityplayer.dll, manifest.json, and awindows[.]storage.dll. A cmd /c line builds a reg add command from chained set variables to write an HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce value pointing at that executable. awindows[.]storage.dll keeps its original signature on disk. After LoadLibraryA, its added .text section is overwritten in memory with shellcode decrypted from manifest.json. Other injection DLLs seen: windows.StateRepository.dll, wmp.dll, mshtml.dll, and ieframe.dll.
- Later stages: Donut Loader runs an APLib-compressed PE loader with a .text0 section and four imports, which loads the LOLD downloader in memory. LOLD has a LOLD_ mutex and config in a .mscfg section, decrypted with a custom SplitMix64 XOR. Decrypted strings reference GhostedHollowing and ElevatedGhostedHollowing. The LOLD C2s were offline at analysis time. Related HTTP traffic on ports 8093, 8080, and 8700 is attributed to Hermes, with paths such as /ws/publisher?deviceId=, /api/client/report, /api/modules/pins, and /chunks/p_{RANDOM}/.
IOCs from the report: LOLD C2 217.60.102[.]123 and 91.92.243[.]204. Distribution domains include guestsisfilesjpmp[.]com, wovplaying[.]help, biklonasmain[.]net, videohostinginsort[.]net, and videovisitors[.]com. Distribution URLs include oz-cloud[.]com/oz-cloud.zip. MD5s: trojanized UnityPlayer.dll AC8547F5AF42DC6932367EBCB162FB0E and LOLD payload 5A0B0BAE87A464228398696517FCF6F5. Full IOC list is in the report.

item.content:encoded:
OXLoader is now loading through DLL hijacking, using copyright-complaint ZIPs and fake activators from GitLab to deliver Remcos, OverLord, PureRAT, Lunex Stealer, LOLD, and Hermes. Malwarebytes reports a rise in activity, and the payload changes by campaign.

- Delivery and lures: Elastic first documented OXLoader in June 2026, with Google Ads pushing CASTLESTEALER. Malwarebytes now sees ZIPs posing as brand-IP complaints, reached through emailed PDFs or Google Sites pages, including Evidence_of_Violation.zip. WinWord.exe is renamed with double extensions like evidence_of_violation.docx.exe and sideloads a malicious msvcr100.dll. Some lures use long-named .bat files that pull a ZIP holding the malicious DLL. Fake activators and cracks on GitLab form a third route.

- Hijack chain: Abused hosts include Qt5Widgets.dll, Qt6Core.dll, SDL3.dll, UnityPlayer.dll, ANCUtility.dll, dbghelp.dll, msvcr100.dll, and WindowsCodecs.dll, paired with executables tied to Microsoft apps, Steam, OBS Studio, and PDF or Word readers. In the GitLab case, a legitimate Take-Two Interactive executable loads a trojanized UnityPlayer.dll. manifest.json holds encrypted shellcode that gets injected into another legitimate DLL. Shellcode on disk can also be named Dependencies.manifest or titles.png. Code is obfuscated with opaque predicates, control flow flattening, and mixed Boolean arithmetic. Malwarebytes traced it with the Sogen emulator.

- Evasion checks: The loader fails WNetAddConnection2W and WNetGetResourceParentW on purpose and looks for error 67 and 487 to spot VMs. It wants 3 or more processors and a display refresh rate of at least 20 Hz, read via powershell Get-WmiObject Win32_VideoController. It also checks GetUserGeoID against a list including Russia 🇷🇺, Belarus 🇧🇾, and Kazakhstan 🇰🇿, and the UI language against Russian 🇷🇺 (0x419). If it flags an analysis environment, it shuts the system down via cmd or jumps to an invalid address. Patching the function at 0x1807999c2 bypasses the checks.

- Persistence and staging: Files are copied to C:\ProgramData\{random 7 characters}\ as the renamed executable (fl studio pro.exe in this case), unityplayer.dll, manifest.json, and awindows[.]storage.dll. A cmd /c line builds a reg add command from chained set variables to write an HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce value pointing at that executable. awindows[.]storage.dll keeps its original signature on disk. After LoadLibraryA, its added .text section is overwritten in memory with shellcode decrypted from manifest.json. Other injection DLLs seen: windows.StateRepository.dll, wmp.dll, mshtml.dll, and ieframe.dll.

- Later stages: Donut Loader runs an APLib-compressed PE loader with a .text0 section and four imports, which loads the LOLD downloader in memory. LOLD has a LOLD_ mutex and config in a .mscfg section, decrypted with a custom SplitMix64 XOR. Decrypted strings reference GhostedHollowing and ElevatedGhostedHollowing. The LOLD C2s were offline at analysis time. Related HTTP traffic on ports 8093, 8080, and 8700 is attributed to Hermes, with paths such as /ws/publisher?deviceId=, /api/client/report, /api/modules/pins, and /chunks/p_{RANDOM}/.

IOCs from the report: LOLD C2 217.60.102[.]123 and 91.92.243[.]204. Distribution domains include guestsisfilesjpmp[.]com, wovplaying[.]help, biklonasmain[.]net, videohostinginsort[.]net, and videovisitors[.]com. Distribution URLs include oz-cloud[.]com/oz-cloud.zip. MD5s: trojanized UnityPlayer.dll AC8547F5AF42DC6932367EBCB162FB0E and LOLD payload 5A0B0BAE87A464228398696517FCF6F5. Full IOC list is in the report.

Takeaway: Hunt for new random-named ProgramData folders holding a renamed executable beside a DLL like unityplayer.dll, manifest.json, and awindows[.]storage.dll, then check HKCU RunOnce for a value pointing into that folder. Look for cmd /c lines that build reg add from chained set variables, and for double-extension executables like .docx.exe launched from extracted archives. Check for powershell querying CurrentRefreshRate. The anti-VM and geo checks mean a sandbox may stay quiet, so rely on disk and registry evidence.

item.title: Hackers Exploited GL.iNet Cloud Flaw to Install Malware on Routers and KVM Devices
item.description:
Attackers abused GL.iNet's GoodCloud remote management service to push a root reverse shell to customer routers and KVMs. The vendor closed the cloud-side hole, but devices already infected are not cleaned by that fix, and the shell's traces vanish on reboot.
- What happened: GL.iNet says it fixed the flaw on Friday and blocked the attacker's access. It has not said how many devices were hit, when attacks began, or how the cloud service was breached. The Hacker News found no CVE for it. RemoteToHome Consulting verified a root reverse shell on a GL-AXT1800 running firmware 4.8.3 with GoodCloud on. It started Friday evening and called out to 170.39.226[.]219. Two more owners reported the same on that model and firmware. On GL-MT6000 units the same command ran but the connection never completed. The hosting provider has since suspended that server and preserved its data.
- Likely mechanism (vendor has not confirmed): RemoteToHome says a handler in the GoodCloud client takes two values from a cloud message and runs them as root through the shell without validation. That code has shipped since at least December 5, 2024 (a GL-MT3000 release) and runs even if the AstroWarp SD-WAN feature is unused. Presence since 2024 does not mean attacks began then. A second, separate cloud client weakness was reported yesterday, and details are withheld until it is fixed.
- KVM side: one owner's infected GL-RM1 pulled a script and two programs from 66.245.219[.]252 starting Thursday, looked up the copycat domain gl-inet[.]top, scanned the local network, and kept talking to 65.20.71[.]131, which the owner suspects is C2. The downloaded files were not kept, and the infection method is unconfirmed. Whether computers attached to infected KVMs were affected is still under investigation. On other routers, a one-off command searched for KVM implant files and reported back to the same address.
- Evidence fragility: the shell leaves no files behind and its traces disappear at restart. The vendor's marker is a running process containing the exact text crond -i /tmp/.log, but it was absent on the router with the verified shell, so a clean check is not proof of a clean device. Check via LuCI (Status, Processes, search tmp/.log), via SSH with ps | grep tmp, or on the KVM's own terminal (ps -a | grep tmp on RMQ1, ps -aux | grep tmp on others). Run it on the KVM, not the attached computer. A grep line matching only itself is not a hit.
- Remediation gap: GL.iNet's updated notice says the new stable firmware removes the malware without a factory reset, with settings kept. RemoteToHome disagrees. In its RM1 analysis, upgrading with settings kept carried over the password file, SSH keys and a user directory holding scripts that run at every boot. Whether a planted script survives was not tested. Their advice for suspect devices is a firmware reinstall without keeping settings and treating VPN keys, Wi-Fi and admin passwords, cloud credentials and SSH keys as exposed. Fixed versions per model are in the vendor notice, for example 4.8.4 for GL-AXT1800 and 1.10.3 for RM1.
- Separate finding: the same investigation found an older, unrelated backdoor on 49 managed routers, installed in batches between September 2025 and May 2026 by an unknown route. Nothing links it to last week's attacks.
Takeaway: if you suspect a device, do not reboot or upgrade first. Capture the process list before anything else. Before running netstat, confirm /bin/netstat is still a link to busybox, since a swapped copy can start the malware. Then hunt egress and DNS logs for the three IPs and gl-inet[.]top above. Fuller indicators are in RemoteToHome's detailed findings. For confirmed or probable compromise, reinstall firmware without keeping settings and rotate every secret the device held. If GoodCloud must go off until you patch, secure another access path first, and remember that turning it off does not clean an infected device.

item.title: Actively Exploited VMware vCenter Authentication Bypass (CVE-2026-123890): 20261120017
item.description:
Zero-day exploited since September 2026: CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) lets unauthenticated attackers become administrator[@]vsphere.local on VMware vCenter. Patching does not evict an intruder already inside.
Broadcom patched it on 19 November 2026 in VMSA-2026-0009. Google Threat Intelligence / Mandiant reported it privately and attributes exploitation to a suspected China-nexus espionage actor it tracks as ARMORY CASTLE, using a custom tool called BONESAW. It is not yet in CISA KEV, and BtCIRT's advisory says it knows of no confirmed exploitation in Bhutan 🇧🇹.
- The flaw is in the vmdir component. It is a weakness in SRP-6a authentication over DCE/RPC on TCP 2012: session-key disclosure plus predictable identifier generation lets an attacker authenticate with no password. No workaround exists. Systems already patched for the earlier CVE-2026-59309 are still vulnerable. vCenter 7.0 and earlier have no public patch. Fixed builds: 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, 8.0 U3m, and VCF 5.2.5. ESX/ESXi itself is not affected.
- Attack chain in Mandiant's intrusion: the actor exploited a separate BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw to land on an internal appliance, then reached vCenter port 2012 from inside. An instance that is not internet-facing is not automatically safe. BONESAW streamed the directory database (/storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb), pulled the STS SAML private signing key, created a backdoor SSO admin (a local account named sps-<…>[@]vsphere.local), and forged SAML assertions for Global Administrator on the vCenter root object.
- Expansion: the actor enabled SSH on the appliance through the VAMI API (PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh), logged in with the new account, and took the vCenter master encryption key and PostgreSQL credentials. Golden-SAML forgery bypassed MFA. They then logged into ESXi as vpxuser, then root over SSH, browsed VMFS datastores directly, and extracted NTDS.dit, SYSTEM, and SECURITY from a Windows guest's virtual disk before exfiltration.
- Persistence: a backdoored Dropbear SSH server (BEARBONES) listening on TCP 53 and later TCP 33992, presenting the banner SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345, plus a Go/Slack-based implant (LAZYBONES) at /usr/bin/vmtoolscs, restarted by a systemd service. Files to look for: /tmp/123 (BONESAW), /tmp/sss (SAWSNAKE), /tmp/dbr (BEARBONES), and web shells ActiveSer.jsp or u.jsp.
- The same advisory covers four more CVEs: CVE-2026-123891, CVE-2026-123892, and CVE-2026-123893 in SDDC Manager, and CVE-2026-123894 in VMware Tools for Windows. Telco Cloud guidance is in Broadcom KB463116.
Takeaway: treat any exposed vCenter as potentially compromised and hunt before and after patching. Look for new SSO accounts matching sps-<…>[@]vsphere.local, unexplained Global Administrator grants on the root folder, VAMI SSH-enable calls, SSH logins that follow them, listeners on TCP 53 or 33992, the SSH banner above, and ESXi root SSH logins. Forged SAML trust and stolen credentials outlive the patch. If you find hits, start incident response. Restrict TCP 2012, 443, 5480, and 22 to trusted admin hosts. Mandiant's report publishes the attacker IPs, file hashes, and YARA/detection rules.

item.title: An AI agent was aimed at Ukraine's police network. It never got in, but it emptied a platform for town councils on the way
item.description:
An autonomous AI agent called Numa, run from a Russia 🇷🇺 hosted server, went after Ukraine's 🇺🇦 National Police, never got in, and on the way breached a municipal website platform and took 3.7 GB of town council files.
- The operator's working directory was open at 193.178.159[.]122 (ports 8000 and 8081): 31,367 files, 9.9 GB, found 22 November 2026. It also holds 80 agent sessions from October 2026, 14 of them against Ukrainian 🇺🇦 sites. Nothing in the files shows authorisation from the organisations concerned.
- Entry was an October CMS council site: the agent mined a 64.9 GB application log the web server handed out, using HTTP Range requests for keys and connection strings. It then used CVE-2021-32648, a loose comparison where a JSON boolean true in the reset code field passes. The flaw was fixed in build 472 and 1.1.5 and has been on CISA's KEV list since 18 January 2022. The platform database dates it: the council admin record changed 18 November 19:20:17, and a new admin (first name Numa, last name Audit) appeared at 19:27:25. A mail template then gave command execution through a Twig reduce filter calling a PHP function, with output written to a text file under site storage (T1190).
- Persistence: gs-netcat from the gsocket relay network, saved as php-fpm7.2 in a hidden .fpm folder inside the application cache, with a launcher named start and a crontab line running it (T1036.005, T1053.003). It dials out, so there is no listening port and no inbound login to see.
- Collection: a production database export, documents, archives and 3,123 images from up to eleven councils, the uploads pulled in 50 MB parts, each checked on arrival (T1030). The operator's scripts built a personal-data index with OCR and Ukrainian 🇺🇦 keyword lists: 12,243 surname matches, 5,576 street addresses, 815 phone numbers. One script checks whether military keywords reflect real conscription data.
- Police perimeter: 98 probe folders on 21 and 22 November, at least six published CVEs tested read-only, five VPN protocols probed, router default account tried. Source-address allowlists and MFA on remote access held, and the agent's reports end by asking a human for one working account.
Takeaway: the agent signs its work, which helps hunters. Search web logs for POST to /backend/backend/auth/reset/<id> across ids 1 to 10, status 206 reads of storage/logs, and fetches of g<8 hex>.txt, ev_<8 hex>_*.txt or numa<8 hex>.php from site storage. On disk, look for the .fpm folder under storage/framework/cache, a process whose binary sits in a cache or storage path, and cron lines running .fpm/start. Query stored mail templates for list filters calling system or exec, and backend users with first name Numa or a login beginning numa. The report notes the queries are unrun against victims; the full hunt set and IOC table are in the report.

item.title: Hackers exploit GL.iNet cloud flaw to infect routers, KVM devices
item.description:
GL.iNet confirmed that attackers abused a flaw in its GoodCloud remote management service to push custom malware onto customers' routers and KVM devices. Some owners report backdoors and root reverse shells, and the cloud fix does not clean devices that are already infected.
- Scope and status: GL.iNet's November 20 advisory says the attack path is blocked and the cloud vulnerability fixed, but it has not disclosed the exploitation method, the number of victims, or whether data was stolen. It is also investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were compromised. Stable firmware with further fixes is scheduled for November 22. KVM guidance is 1.10.3 or later for RM10, RM1, RM1V2, RM1PE and RM4PE, 1.10.3 beta or later for RM10RC, and 1.8.7 or later for RMQ1.
- The installer: BleepingComputer analyzed a ni[.]sh script that recognizes many GL.iNet models and pulls executables named gl-helper and gb from hardcoded servers. It persists through startup scripts and scheduled tasks, disguises its process as crond -i /tmp/.log (GL.iNet's published IOC), plants SSH public keys, modifies file timestamps, and polls a remote server for commands. It also swaps netstat for a shell script that filters out connections to 66.245.219[.]252. Chinese-language developer comments suggest a Chinese-speaking author.
- Infrastructure and behavior: ni[.]sh and the payloads came from 66.245.219[.]252 on November 19 in a GL-RM1 owner's network logs. A second address, 65.20.71[.]131, is also in the script and those logs. Other victims showed root reverse shells built on the Linux nc utility connecting to 170.39.226[.]219. The GL-RM1 owner also saw about 1,800 residential IPs contacted daily plus repeated calls to the TRON blockchain API, which looks peer-to-peer, but the purpose is unconfirmed. A GL-MT2500 router carried a Lua payload launched via a modified urandom_seed startup script that collects device info and downloads more programs.
- Field data, with caveats: RemoteToHome Consulting checked 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152. That included 24 root reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 with evidence of attacker-supplied commands. They note this may not match other customers and the older backdoors may be unrelated. They also flagged a possible root command injection in a GoodCloud client handler for AstroWarp/SD-WAN, but GL.iNet has not confirmed it was used. Some malware files carried December 2025 timestamps, though timestamps are attacker-modifiable and the link to this incident is unclear.
- Detection gaps: forum members warn the crond -i /tmp/.log check may miss devices with other backdoors or reverse shells. A community-built scanner, linked from GL.iNet's support instructions, checks known malware files, suspicious processes, modified system utilities, and persistence-modified config files, and can collect forensic evidence. Its developers say it cannot catch every infection, and malicious files in config directories can survive an ordinary firmware upgrade.
Takeaway: do not trust on-device netstat output on a suspect unit, since the malware filters its own traffic. Check egress from the firewall or upstream NetFlow for 66.245.219[.]252, 65.20.71[.]131 and 170.39.226[.]219, and look for nc outbound sessions. Preserve evidence first by running the scanner's collection, or imaging the device, before any reset. Then reflash firmware without retaining settings, do not restore old configs, and rotate credentials and access keys. For KVM units, treat the attached hosts as in scope and review them as well. The IOC process string and IPs are in the report.

item.content:encoded:
GL.iNet confirmed that attackers abused a flaw in its GoodCloud remote management service to push custom malware onto customers' routers and KVM devices. Some owners report backdoors and root reverse shells, and the cloud fix does not clean devices that are already infected.

- Scope and status: GL.iNet's November 20 advisory says the attack path is blocked and the cloud vulnerability fixed, but it has not disclosed the exploitation method, the number of victims, or whether data was stolen. It is also investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were compromised. Stable firmware with further fixes is scheduled for November 22. KVM guidance is 1.10.3 or later for RM10, RM1, RM1V2, RM1PE and RM4PE, 1.10.3 beta or later for RM10RC, and 1.8.7 or later for RMQ1.

- The installer: BleepingComputer analyzed a ni[.]sh script that recognizes many GL.iNet models and pulls executables named gl-helper and gb from hardcoded servers. It persists through startup scripts and scheduled tasks, disguises its process as crond -i /tmp/.log (GL.iNet's published IOC), plants SSH public keys, modifies file timestamps, and polls a remote server for commands. It also swaps netstat for a shell script that filters out connections to 66.245.219[.]252. Chinese-language developer comments suggest a Chinese-speaking author.

- Infrastructure and behavior: ni[.]sh and the payloads came from 66.245.219[.]252 on November 19 in a GL-RM1 owner's network logs. A second address, 65.20.71[.]131, is also in the script and those logs. Other victims showed root reverse shells built on the Linux nc utility connecting to 170.39.226[.]219. The GL-RM1 owner also saw about 1,800 residential IPs contacted daily plus repeated calls to the TRON blockchain API, which looks peer-to-peer, but the purpose is unconfirmed. A GL-MT2500 router carried a Lua payload launched via a modified urandom_seed startup script that collects device info and downloads more programs.

- Field data, with caveats: RemoteToHome Consulting checked 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152. That included 24 root reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 with evidence of attacker-supplied commands. They note this may not match other customers and the older backdoors may be unrelated. They also flagged a possible root command injection in a GoodCloud client handler for AstroWarp/SD-WAN, but GL.iNet has not confirmed it was used. Some malware files carried December 2025 timestamps, though timestamps are attacker-modifiable and the link to this incident is unclear.

- Detection gaps: forum members warn the crond -i /tmp/.log check may miss devices with other backdoors or reverse shells. A community-built scanner, linked from GL.iNet's support instructions, checks known malware files, suspicious processes, modified system utilities, and persistence-modified config files, and can collect forensic evidence. Its developers say it cannot catch every infection, and malicious files in config directories can survive an ordinary firmware upgrade.

Takeaway: do not trust on-device netstat output on a suspect unit, since the malware filters its own traffic. Check egress from the firewall or upstream NetFlow for 66.245.219[.]252, 65.20.71[.]131 and 170.39.226[.]219, and look for nc outbound sessions. Preserve evidence first by running the scanner's collection, or imaging the device, before any reset. Then reflash firmware without retaining settings, do not restore old configs, and rotate credentials and access keys. For KVM units, treat the attached hosts as in scope and review them as well. The IOC process string and IPs are in the report.

item.title: AI AGENTIC PENTEST FRAMEWORK IN THE WILD
item.description:
Open-source agentic pentest frameworks, led by ARTEX, are now showing up in real intrusions and on thousands of exposed hosts. The Raven File tracked about 8400 unique IPs across six frameworks and found overlaps with ransomware, RAT and C2 infrastructure.
- ARTEX is an open-source autonomous pentest framework released on GitHub in July 2026 by a Chinese 🇨🇳 developer. A planning agent picks the next action, worker agents run nmap, curl and Impacket, and results feed a shared graph of assets and findings. Reported adopters: Storm-0940 (ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply chain, 2,250+ downstream tenants, sign-in attempts peaking at 2,900 per minute), Vapor Panda (200+ orgs in 14+ countries) and Onyx Sleet. Separately, CL-STA-1238 paired Cairn with Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek for 25 operations against 19 orgs and 10 breaches. Barracuda said an attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours, and its probe names and credential-hunting routines matched ARTEX.
- A live Cairn demo shows what the agent does by default. Given only "Pentest the dify[.]ai" and no scope or rules, it produced 50+ sequential intents: local recon, public SaaS testing, supply-chain analysis, static reverse engineering of Dify EE images and the Helm chart, default JWT and credential tests, and repeated subdomain takeover attempts against forum.dify[.]ai and dev-kyoukai.langgenius[.]app. The report maps this to T1595, T1190, T1078, T1110, T1552.001 and T1583.001. Expect persistent, methodical, noisy traffic, not one-shot scans.
- Other reported cases: Cairn found an unpatched path traversal (GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94) in MONAI Label and wrote a Python reverse shell within 11 minutes. An e-commerce campaign ran 1,100+ parallel web-attack projects at about $5 per task against 100+ companies, planting web shells and stealing card data via a Magento flaw (CVE-2026-75650, StyleSmuggler), misconfigured upload endpoints, legacy Zend PHP deserialization and memcached unauthorized write. Seven South Korean 🇰🇷 financial institutions lost data on roughly 67,000 to 68,000 people. The report stresses humans stay in the loop for key decisions.
- Infrastructure: the panels are fingerprintable. ARTEX (3800+ hosts) uses the title ARTEX - 自主渗透测试控制台, FOFA icon_hash -576220750, top port 8787. Other FOFA icon hashes: AntiFox -1356779733, CyberStrike -1349384020, PentAGI -1596753120, Cairn 762324858. Daily growth: ARTEX 144 hosts, PentAGI 43, CyberStrike 36, Cairn 23. 97 IPs run three frameworks at once, 82 of them in 91.224.92.0/24 at Lithuanian 🇱🇹 UAB Host Baltic (AS209605).
- Overlaps: 81 IPs also host Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, AdaptixC2, Supershell or VShell. Examples: 31.59.220[.]14 (Emperador ransomware file server plus ARTEX), 45.77.179[.]49 (DCRat plus ARTEX), 91.224.92[.]203 (Kimwolf Android botnet plus ARTEX), 111.68.4[.]13 (Chinese 🇨🇳 actor attacking ConnectWise plus ARTEX). Caveat from the report: many hosts are honeypots, and not every panel is malicious.
Takeaway: the per-framework IP lists are in the author's GitHub Daily-Hunt repository, referenced in the report. Enrich them against your firewall, proxy and auth logs, then look at what hit you. Hunt for high-rate sign-in bursts, default-credential attempts and sequential probing of OpenAPI, SSO and admin routes from one source. Audit your DNS for dangling CNAMEs, since subdomain takeover was a recurring agent goal. Rotate any secrets shipped in public charts or images. Treat a hit on a known C2 IP that also serves one of these panels as higher confidence than a panel alone.

item.title: Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets
item.description:
Rackspace Spot was breached on November 17 with leaked credentials, letting attackers create pods and read Kubernetes Secrets in customer clusters. Assume every Secret in affected clusters is exposed.
- Access and timeline: Per Rackspace's customer notification, obtained by BleepingComputer, an unauthorized party used leaked credentials to reach parts of the Rackspace Spot platform on November 17, 2026, between about 00:20 and 22:00 UTC. Rackspace learned of it on November 18 from a customer report and confirmed that customer's organization was affected the same day. The report does not say how the credentials leaked.
- What the attackers could do: They acted as legitimate users in some customer organizations. That allowed them to create pods in Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes. Rackspace warns they could have read any Secret in an affected user's clusters, plus any Spot API tokens or refresh tokens that user held. Secrets commonly hold passwords, auth tokens, and API keys for databases, cloud services, and other systems, so the blast radius extends beyond Spot.
- Indicators in the report: IP address 23.224.79[.]106 and the range 23.224.0[.]0/15. Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object name prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe. Rackspace has not said how many customers were affected or whether customer data was stolen. BleepingComputer asked and had no response at publication.
- Response and outage: Rackspace says it revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and tightened access controls and monitoring. The Spot admin console had an extended outage. Platform9 co-founder Sirish Raghuram said on Reddit that access was deliberately shut off while the environment was sanitized. That outage temporarily kept customers from managing clusters and rotating credentials. Rackspace announced full restoration on November 21.
- Customer actions required: Reissue Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens used in automation tools, download fresh Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate every credential stored in cluster Secrets. Rackspace also tells customers to analyze logs for databases, container registries, Git repositories, cloud storage, and third-party services back to November 17 to spot abuse of exposed credentials.
Takeaway: Treat this as a credential-exposure investigation, not just a rotation task. Search your clusters for pods, objects, and volumes with the i1, glm-, and probe prefixes, and check for any pod you did not create on or after November 17. Look for pod creation, Secret reads, and node or volume listing activity in that window. Search every downstream system's logs for 23.224.79[.]106 and the 23.224.0[.]0/15 range, then trace any use of credentials that lived in cluster Secrets. Preserve cluster state and logs before cleanup. The IOCs are in Rackspace's customer notification as reported by BleepingComputer. No detection rules are mentioned.

item.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
item.description:
